This week's papers keep asking whether an apparent specific deficit is really something more general. In [a forced-response flanker study of over 200 younger and older adults](#p3), age differences in inhibitory control were explained by global slowing, with no selective inhibition deficit. [Work on resampling rejected hypotheses](#p6) found that attention control accounted for the working memory link, which suggests the problem is disengaging from outdated ideas rather than remembering a list of them. papers.title: Day by day, bit by bit: Knowledge building mechanisms evolve with development
papers.authors: Layla Unger, Olivera Savic, Vladimir M. Sloutsky
papers.summary: Four- to six-year-olds were exposed repeatedly over a month to regularities among words, to see whether they could build up connected word knowledge across encounters. Younger children seemed to relearn the regularities from scratch each time, while older children strengthened connections a bit more with every exposure. It points to a real developmental shift in how gradual, cumulative learning works.
papers.abstract: Much of human knowledge distills patterns that are consistent across many similar experiences over time, such as the typical layout of a bedroom. This is particularly true of word knowledge. The thousands of words we learn form a stable, interconnected network of word meanings that capture regularities in the way words are typically combined to express ideas, such as that "oranges" are something you can "eat" and similar to "apples". Yet, we know surprisingly little about accumulating knowledge from regularities over time, especially in childhood when building knowledge is paramount. Here, we investigated 4-6-year-old children's abilities to accumulate interconnected word knowledge from regularities experienced repeatedly over a month. Younger children appeared to relearn the regularities anew at each exposure, whereas older children accumulated increasingly strong connections across encounters. These findings point to substantial developmental changes in gradual learning processes that build knowledge over time.

papers.title: Modeling working memory capacity in sentence processing with lossy-context surprisal
papers.authors: Jiaxin Li, Michael Hahn, Vera Demberg
papers.abstract: Understanding how comprehenders interpret linguistic input in real time has long been a focus of sentence processing research. The recently-proposed Resource-Rational Lossy-context Surprisal (RR-LCS) model can be applied for making predictions at the level of individual readers: it predicts that individuals with low working memory capacity (WMC) have a lossy representation of the previous context and may therefore experience high surprisal at a long-distance dependency, while individuals with high WMC will experience a lower surprisal effect as this dependent to them may still be highly predictable from previous context. To date, these predictions have not been empirically tested. Here, we evaluate them using a controlled A-Maze task (Experiment 1) and an analysis of reading more naturalistic text based on the InDiCo corpus (Experiment 2). In Experiment 1, we investigated how WMC influences sentence processing across short, long, and very long dependency conditions. The results revealed that low-WMC participants initially showed a strong locality effect between the short and long conditions, which decreased over time due to adaptation. High-WMC participants demonstrated locality effects between both the short-long and long-very long conditions from the start, with these effects gradually diminishing as their memory allocation became more efficient. These findings align with the RR-LCS model’s predictions, showing that high-WMC individuals maintained larger context sizes, such that they could more easily process long-distance dependencies, whereas low-WMC individuals, constrained by smaller context sizes, experienced pronounced locality effects. Experiment 2 confirmed that WMC modulates sensitivity to lossy-context surprisal (LCS), with LCS improving model fit particularly strongly for low-WMC participants. These findings underscore the significance of individual differences in WMC for processing complex syntactic structures. By combining experimental data with computational modeling, we provide a deeper understanding of how WMC shapes language comprehension.
papers.summary: A recent model of sentence processing (Resource-Rational Lossy-context Surprisal) predicts that people with lower working memory capacity keep a fuzzier record of earlier words, so long-distance dependencies should hit them harder. The researchers tested this with a controlled A-Maze reading task and with naturalistic reading data from the InDiCo corpus. Low-WMC readers showed strong locality effects (extra difficulty when dependencies are longer) that faded as they adapted, while high-WMC readers showed such effects across longer distances and also adapted over time. Lossy-context surprisal also improved model fit most for low-WMC readers, which makes this a nice link between individual differences and a computational account.

papers.title: Dimensional asymmetries in social attention: Dynamic head movements elicit opposite attentional biases in vertical versus horizontal dimensions
papers.authors: Felix J. Götz, Paul M. Heineck, Anne Böckler et al.
papers.summary: When a face turns its head while looking straight at you, your attention often jumps the opposite way from the head turn, which is called the overshoot effect. Across four preregistered experiments, vertical head movements produced attention shifts in the same direction as the head, while horizontal movements gave the classic opposite-direction overshoot. Closing the eyes strengthened both effects, so direct gaze dampens head cues but doesn't flip their direction, which suggests social attention treats vertical and horizontal cues differently.
papers.abstract: When observing a person with direct gaze but a horizontally averted head posture, attention often shifts opposite to head direction (overshoot effect). We investigated whether this effect generalizes to vertical head movements and whether it depends on gaze direction information. Across four experiments, centrally presented faces shifted dynamically to averted head positions before a target appeared at a location congruent or incongruent with head direction. Vertical head movements (Experiments 1 and 2) produced head-congruency effects, which were stronger when the eyes were closed. In contrast, horizontal head movements (Experiments 3 and 4) produced classic overshoot effects, which surprisingly were amplified when the eyes were closed. Thus, direct gaze attenuated head-cueing effects but did not alter their direction. Overall, these findings reveal dimensional asymmetries in social attention and demonstrate that gaze-head integration considers spatial context. Implications for hierarchical, holistic, and predictive cue-integration accounts are discussed. Open Practices Statement All four experiments were preregistered on the Open Science Framework (OSF; Experiment 1: https://osf.io/qds4x ; Experiment 2: https://osf.io/d6rwe ; Experiment 3: https://osf.io/xe9a6 ; Experiment 4: https://osf.io/3pq49 ). Materials, experimental scripts, stimuli, raw data, and analysis scripts underlying the reported results are publicly available at https://osf.io/aq7zf/ and https://osf.io/j96fx/

papers.title: Does Global Slowing Explain Age Effects in Inhibitory Control?
papers.authors: Jacob Sellers, Han Zhang, John Jonides et al.
papers.summary: Do older adults have a specific problem with inhibitory control, or are they just slower across the board? Over 200 younger and older adults did a forced-response arrow-flanker task, and a computational model was used to separate the component processes. The results showed global slowing with no selective inhibition deficit, and that slowing alone could account for the mixed results in earlier studies using free response times.
papers.abstract: A long-standing debate in the study of cognitive aging centers around the issue of whether aging results in a selective deficit in inhibitory control beyond general slowing of cognitive processing. Previous studies have obtained mixed findings, in part because the typical free-response-time paradigm lacks the specificity required to disentangle component processes underlying inhibitory control. Here, we apply a forced-response paradigm and computational model to test whether aging results in overall speed differences or a selective deficit in inhibitory control. Across two experiments, over 200 older adults and younger adults completed a forced-response arrow-flanker task. We found strong evidence that older adults demonstrate a global slowing of processing without any selective deficit in inhibitory control in this task. Furthermore, we demonstrate that global slowing is sufficient to explain the mixed findings in previous free-response-time studies. Overall, these results argue against a selective inhibitory-control deficit in older adults.

papers.title: Language Models Share a Readout Bottleneck in Working Memory
papers.authors: Dongyu Gong
papers.summary: Large language models show the same working-memory pattern humans do on the N-back task: worse performance as load rises, with errors clustering on lures. Testing 15 pretrained models plus small transformers trained from scratch, the researchers found that attention heads usually do locate the right item, and linear probes can decode the correct answer even when the model false-alarms. Suppressing the identity of competing items helped, while sharpening attention didn't, so the bottleneck seems to be reading out under interference rather than finding the item, echoing interference accounts of human working memory.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) reproduce a human working-memory signature on the N-back task: performance declines as memory load N increases, and errors concentrate on lures, items that repeat the current stimulus at a neighboring but incorrect serial position. We ask whether this shared behavioral signature reflects a shared mechanism. The literature offers two candidate accounts. On a precision account, softmax attention cannot concentrate its weight on the item N positions back, so adjacent items are retrieved instead. On an interference account, attention selects the correct item, but the content of competing items corrupts the decision. We dissociate these accounts in 15 pretrained LLMs from three families (70 million to 14 billion parameters) and in minimal transformers trained from scratch. In all three families, the attention heads that carry the task attend to the target on most missed matches. Linear probes decode near-perfectly whether a matching letter occurred at the target or at a lure position, even on trials where the model false-alarms to the lure, although its own decisions barely distinguish the two. Sharpening attention yields negligible gains, whereas suppressing the letter identity of non-target items improves sensitivity (d') in nearly all model-by-load conditions. In larger models the task is spread over more heads, and removing interference helps more. In minimal transformers, precision limits a single attention layer, but a second layer removes this constraint. The working-memory limit of LLMs therefore lies in reading items out under interference rather than in locating them, consistent with interference accounts of human working memory.

papers.title: No Evidence that Retrieval Practice Facilitates Cortical Memory Integration: Insights from Novel Word Semantic Priming
papers.authors: Lewis Vincent Ball, M. Gareth Gaskell
papers.summary: One idea, the Rapid Consolidation Hypothesis, says retrieving new information helps it integrate into cortical knowledge networks. To test it, participants learned novel words like "blontack" by either restudying or retrieving definitions, then did a primed lexical decision task right away and about 48 hours later. Retrieval practice improved definition recall at 48 hours, but novel words showed no semantic priming in either condition, with Bayesian analyses moderately favoring no effect. So retrieval helps retention but may not drive integration, though the authors note methodological limits that could have made priming hard to detect.
papers.abstract: According to the Rapid Consolidation Hypothesis (RCH), retrieving new information from memory integrates the corresponding memory representations into cortical long-term memory, leading to longer-term memory benefits than restudy or rehearsal. However, this prediction has not been empirically tested. We explored this in the current study by comparing semantic priming effects between novel words taught under retrieval practice and restudy conditions. Words are more effective at priming (speeding up) the recognition of semantically related words once they have integrated with related knowledge in cortical language networks. According to the RCH, semantic priming should therefore be enhanced for novel words taught via retrieval practice. In a learning phase, participants learned 20 novel words and their definitions (e.g., blontack - a type of cat) under restudy conditions and 20 under retrieval practice conditions by retrieving part of the definition (e.g., blontack - a type of ___). The novel words, and a set of familiar words, then served as prime words for related (e.g., dog) and unrelated target words in a primed lexical decision task, both immediately after learning and ~48 hrs later. Familiar prime words successfully primed the recognition of related target words in both tasks. The definitions of novel words taught under retrieval practice were recalled more accurately ~48 hrs later than the restudy condition. However, we found no significant priming effects in either learning condition or task, with exploratory Bayesian analyses revealing moderate evidence in favour of the null hypothesis. Our findings suggest that retrieval practice facilitates the longer-term retention of novel words and their definitions, but may not support their integration with related knowledge in language networks. However, methodological factors could have attenuated the scope for semantic priming with novel words, with future research required to continue this investigation.

papers.title: Memory and Cognitive Control in Hypothesis Sampling: Individual Differences in Resampling Rejected Hypotheses
papers.authors: Yoonsang Lee, Randall W Engle
papers.summary: When testing hypotheses, people sometimes return to ones they've already ruled out. In 302 participants, higher working memory, fluid intelligence, and attention control each went with less resampling, but only fluid intelligence held up as a unique predictor once the three were separated. Attention control accounted for the working memory link, which fits the idea that avoiding rejected hypotheses is more about disengaging from outdated ideas than about holding a list of them in memory.
papers.abstract: Efficient hypothesis sampling requires avoiding resampling: returning to hypotheses that have already been rejected. Doing so could depend on maintaining information about which hypotheses have been ruled out, or on disengaging from previously activated hypotheses once they are no longer relevant. Participants (N = 302) completed a hypothe- sis sampling task in which they tested hypotheses from six alternatives until identifying the correct one, along with batteries measuring working memory capacity (WMC), fluid intelligence (Gf), and attention control (AC). In latent- variable models, higher WMC, Gf, and AC were each associated with less resampling when considered separately, but only Gf uniquely predicted resampling once their overlapping contributions were partialled out. Mediation anal- yses showed that AC accounted for the WMC association but not the Gf association. Separating AC into selective and sustained components, selective but not sustained AC predicted resampling, although not uniquely after ac- counting for Gf and WMC, and neither component mediated the Gf effect. Overall, this pattern is consistent with the idea that avoiding rejected hypotheses depends more on disengaging from outdated representations than on maintaining information in working memory. The unique Gf association beyond AC suggests that this contributionis not fully reducible to domain-general attention control.

papers.title: Statistical Learning of Distractor Suppression Generalizes Across Contexts Despite Blocked Learning
papers.authors: Milan Geldhof, Brent Vernaillen, Christophe Vanhouwe et al.
papers.summary: People can learn to suppress locations where distractors often appear, and this learning is sometimes tied to context. Here, 136 participants learned with each background color paired with a distractor location in uninterrupted blocks, then were tested with equal distractor probabilities. Background color made no difference to response times, and Bayesian analyses decisively favored context-independent suppression. Even with repeated, blocked pairings, the learned suppression seems to be robust and to carry across contexts.
papers.abstract: Statistical learning can shape visual attention by enabling spatial suppression of locations that frequently contain distractors. Although learned suppression may be context-dependent, the underlying factors driving this dependency remain unclear. While previous research has largely focused on the nature of the context itself, less attention has been paid to how context–regularity pairs are presented, particularly whether they are blocked or intermixed across trials. Multiple uninterrupted pairings may be necessary for less salient contextual cues, such as background colors or images, to support context-dependent learning. The present preregistered, high- powered study (N = 136) therefore used a blocked presentation, with two blocks each pairing a unique background color with a high-frequency distractor location, followed by an intermixed testing phase with equiprobable distractor locations. Results show that although distractors reliably captured attention, the background context did not affect response times in the testing block, with Bayesian analyses providing decisive evidence for context-independent suppression. These results show that implicitly learned distractor suppression is highly robust, persistent, and generalizes across non-task- relevant contexts, even when context–regularity associations are repeated and uninterrupted during learning.

papers.title: A deer in the elevator. The effect of information congruency on immediate recall and delayed recognition
papers.authors: Lucie Guštarová, Jan Chromý
papers.summary: Using four self-paced reading experiments in Czech, researchers asked whether sentence content that fits expectations, like a deer in a forest versus in an elevator, is encoded better. Congruent locations were recalled more accurately right after reading, but a delayed recognition test showed no reliable congruency advantage. The pattern suggests incongruent information has a higher bar for getting encoded, but once it gets in, it's no worse off later.
papers.abstract: This study investigates how information congruency influences memory during sentence comprehension. Although previous research has shown that congruent information facilitates comprehension, it remains unclear whether this advantage arises already at the earliest stages of memory encoding. We addressed this question in four self-paced reading experiments in Czech, manipulating location congruency (congruent vs. incongruent), type of information targeted by the comprehension question (agent vs. location), and sentence position (initial vs. medial), and combining an immediate recall task with a delayed word recognition test. Across experiments, congruent locations were recalled more accurately than incongruent ones immediately after sentence processing, indicating a robust congruency advantage in early encoding outcomes. In contrast, delayed recognition showed no reliable congruency advantage, suggesting that the effect is primarily restricted to early encoding processes. If a piece of information is already encoded while the sentence is being read, it appears to be largely unaffected by congruency afterwards. Thus, incongruent information must pass a higher threshold to be encoded, but once it is successfully encoded, it is no longer disadvantaged.

papers.title: A Computational Swinging Lexical Network: Cohort Concentration Predicts Semantic Interference in a Large-Scale Picture–Word Interference Dataset
papers.authors: Louis Schiekiera, Rasha Abdel Rahman, Alissa Melinger et al.
papers.summary: The Swinging Lexical Network model says naming speed depends on how a target and distractor co-activate a cohort of related words. The researchers built it computationally on a 30,000-word semantic network and tested it on 392,156 picture-word interference trials from 86 English and German experiments. Naming was slower when a few words stood out as strongly activated competitors and faster when activation was spread thinly, so competitors seem to be the words that stand out, not every active one. A second measure, the swing, helped fit but was too tangled up with concentration to separate.
papers.abstract: The Swinging Lexical Network (SLN) model explains semantic context effects in word production through the lexical cohort that a target and distractor co-activate: whether naming is facilitated or slowed depends on the balance between semantic priming and lexical competition within this cohort. As a verbal theory the SLN leaves open what counts as a competitor: any co-activated word, or only words whose activation stands out. We implemented the SLN computationally, letting activation spread through a 30,000-word distributional semantic network. From this process we derived two measures. Cohort concentration is the degree to which co-activation falls on a few words instead of being spread thinly across many. The swing is how much the activation pattern still changes over later spreading steps. In a harmonized picture--word interference dataset of 392,156 trials from 86 English and German experiments, cohort concentration was the only semantic predictor with a reliable effect in both languages: naming was slower when a few words stood out as strongly activated competitors and faster when activation was diffuse. Competitors are thus the words whose activation stands out from the background, not every word that receives some activation. Adding the swing improved fit, but its effect could not be separated from cohort concentration, with which it was strongly correlated. Because spreading converges on the same network-wide state for every word pair, later steps largely re-express the initial cohort. In line with the SLN, our computational implementation shows that semantic interference depends on how co-activation is distributed across the cohort.

papers.title: The medial temporal lobe and the retention of scene memories across a one-week delay
papers.authors: Angelique I. Delarazan, Alexis N. Garcia, Ashley Huggins et al.
papers.summary: Fifty-seven healthy older adults watched 360-degree videos of real places and freely recalled each scene soon after and again a week later. The amount of detail recalled didn't change much, but what people remembered became more individual to them, and larger medial temporal lobe volume went with recalling details more consistently with the first recall. Perirhinal cortex volume was especially tied to this consistency, suggesting the MTL helps keep scene details stable over time.
papers.abstract: Remembering everyday events involves retaining multiple components, including the scenes that provide the spatial and contextual setting in which events occur. The medial temporal lobe (MTL) supports scene construction and complex event memory. However, less is known about its contribution to retaining the details of an event’s scene over time, as scene information is typically embedded within narrative and event structures that are assessed for memory shortly after encoding. To examine scene memory retention, fifty-seven cognitively healthy older adults viewed 360-degree panoramic videos depicting real-world environments and freely recalled each scene shortly after viewing and again one week later. We tested whether individual differences in MTL volume were related to retention of scene memory and whether these relationships changed across the one-week delay. The proportion of episodic detail retrieved did not significantly change across the one-week delay, but the details recalled changed and became more participant specific, as measured by several measures of text-based similarity. Critically, relationships between MTL volume and scene memory also changed over time such that greater MTL volume was associated with being more consistent with what was originally recalled. Exploratory subregional analyses further showed that perirhinal cortex volume was robustly associated with the text-based similarity measures. These findings suggest that MTL is related to memory for the scene component of complex experience, particularly the ability to consistently recall the details of a scene over time.

papers.title: Configural Object Novelty Alters Network Coordination Across the Medial Temporal Lobe
papers.authors: Lauren Alexandra Homann, Jennifer D. Ryan, Rosanna K. Olsen et al.
papers.summary: The same features can make a different object if they're combined differently, and the researchers asked how medial temporal lobe regions coordinate when that happens. Using fMRI connectivity analyses in younger adults viewing repeated, recombined, and novel objects, they found that new configurations of familiar features led to widespread drops in connectivity across a hippocampal-cortical network, with a few increases involving posteromedial entorhinal cortex. Novel features alone showed no connectivity differences, suggesting configural novelty engages a broader network than the usual object-processing regions.
papers.abstract: Object identity depends on how constituent features are combined, such that the same features may form distinct objects when their configuration changes. The perirhinal (PRC) and anterolateral entorhinal (alERC) cortices are implicated in such conjunctive object processing; however, regional sensitivity alone cannot reveal how information is coordinated across regions, or whether this coordination extends beyond object-processing regions to spatial and relational regions. Using generalized psychophysiological interaction (gPPI) analysis of BOLD signals extracted from manually-segmented medial temporal lobe regions, we examined task-modulated functional connectivity while younger adults viewed repeated objects (familiar features in familiar configurations), recombined objects (familiar features in novel configurations), and novel objects (novel features in novel configurations). This design permitted isolation of connectivity changes associated with configural, featural, and global object novelty. Configural novelty (repeated vs. recombined objects) was associated with widespread reductions in connectivity spanning anterior-temporal, posterior-medial, and hippocampal regions, extending to medial prefrontal and posterior-medial cortex, alongside more limited increases in connectivity between posteromedial entorhinal cortex (pmERC) and superior parietal and frontal regions. In contrast, featural novelty (recombined vs. novel objects) and global novelty (repeated vs. novel objects) were not associated with significant connectivity differences. These findings demonstrate that configural object novelty alters coordination across a distributed hippocampal-cortical network, with connectivity effects extending beyond the anterior-temporal regions traditionally implicated in object processing, highlighting how object and relational processing systems work in concert to support conjunctive object processing. Connectivity thus provides a complementary window onto how conjunctive information is coordinated, beyond what regional sensitivity alone can reveal.

papers.title: Cognitive forecasting: How intuitive theories of attention shape anticipated risk preferences
papers.authors: Dogukan Demircioglu, Chris Dawson, Samuel G.B. Johnson
papers.abstract: How do people forecast their own and others' risk preferences? Although it is well established that affective forecasts shape decision-making, less is known about where these forecasts come from. Five studies demonstrate that people rely on intuitive theories of attention when forecasting future affect-such as dread and savoring while waiting for a risk to be resolved-with these affective forecasts in turn shaping willingness to take such risks. In Study 1, forecasts of the participant's own expectations and attention were systematically related to forecasts of positive and negative affect during a waiting period, which in turn predicted risk preferences. Studies 2a and 2b demonstrate substantial heterogeneity in intuitive attention-affect theories: some participants believed attention amplifies the emotional consequences of expectations, whereas others believed attention is uniformly affectively negative. These differences led to sharply divergent predictions about when attention should increase or decrease risk-taking. Study 3 shows that attention is also informative about expectations: participants differed in whether they believed attention signals optimism or pessimism, producing downstream consequences for affective forecasts and risk-taking. Finally, Study 4 reveals that many people endorse asymmetric causal models, viewing optimism as a cause of risk-taking, but risk-taking as a cause of attention. Together, these findings show that forecasts of risk preferences depend critically on people's intuitive theories about how cognition shapes affect and how affective utility is generated over time. By integrating affective forecasting, attention, and decision-making under uncertainty, this work highlights the role of metacognitive beliefs in shaping economic preferences.
papers.summary: Across five studies, the researchers asked how people predict their own and others' risk preferences, and found that forecasts draw on intuitive theories about attention. For example, people predict how much dread or savoring they'd feel while waiting for a risk to resolve, and those predictions shape willingness to take the risk. The theories vary a lot between people: some think attention amplifies the emotional effect of expectations, others think attention is just negative, and people also differ on whether attention signals optimism or pessimism. Many also hold an asymmetric causal view, where optimism causes risk-taking but risk-taking causes attention, so metacognitive beliefs seem to matter for economic choices.

papers.title: Grammatical acceptability is affected by the fit between the construction and noun phrase/contextual meaning: Evidence from six pre-registered judgment studies
papers.authors: Ben Ambridge, Aliza Bukhari, I. Made Sena Darmasetiyawan et al.
papers.summary: Why do some understandable sentences, like "The boy dragged the girl the box," sound wrong? Across six preregistered studies, each with 100 participants, English speakers' acceptability ratings were affected both by how well the nouns fit the construction's meaning and by the intended meaning in context, in all but one case. This held across causatives, datives, and active/passive constructions. The authors argue this supports Construction Grammar, where ungrammaticality is a graded semantic clash, over Categorical Grammar accounts that need add-ons to explain gradedness.
papers.abstract: Human language allows for virtually limitless productivity. Why, then, are certain perfectly-comprehensible sentences (e.g., *The boy dragged the girl the box) deemed ungrammatical by native speakers? Here, we test the prediction of Construction Grammar accounts (c.f., Categorical Grammar accounts) that grammatical acceptability is probabilistically affected by the compatibility between the meaning (semantics) of the construction (e.g., [AGENT] [ACTION] [RECPIENT] [PATIENT]) and (a) the nouns (e.g., The boy sent the girl the package is more grammatical than *The boy sent Chicago the package; Studies 1,3,5) and (b) the speaker's intended meaning in context (e.g., the team in the Chicago office > the geographic location; Studies 2,4,6). Across a series of six large (N = 100) pre-registered studies, we find that (in all but one case), both of these factors significantly affect English speakers' rated acceptability of sentences, across the transitive and periphrastic causative (e.g., The clown made the man laugh vs *The clown laughed the man); the to- and double-object dative (e.g., The girl said something to the boy vs *The girl said the boy something) and the active/passive (e.g., The book cost $10 vs *$10 was cost by the book). These findings constitute support for Construction Gramar approaches, under which this type of grammatical acceptability results from a probabilistic semantic clash, and against Categorical Grammar accounts, which can explain graded (as opposed to categorical) ungrammaticality only via some kind of add-on.

papers.title: Word segmentation abilities across the adult lifespan: Evidence from younger and older adult bilinguals
papers.authors: Patricia Fuente-García, Julián Villegas, Adam Zawiszewski et al.
papers.summary: Younger and older Basque-Spanish bilinguals did a phoneme localization task in Basque to test how they use meaning, grammar, and sound cues to segment speech. Age made no difference to segmentation, while second-language proficiency mattered, with the biggest gains when all cues were available. Native speakers benefited more than non-natives from some cues. Language switching and fluid intelligence helped only a little, and overall the results suggest segmentation abilities stay stable across adulthood.
papers.abstract: Humans break down continuous speech into meaningful units by integrating multiple cues whose importance and relative weight change throughout development. We investigate whether segmentation abilities differ between younger and older adults while exploring how age of acquisition, proficiency, language use, and frequency of language switch determine Basque-Spanish younger and older bilinguals' use of lexico-semantic, morphosyntactic, and phonological information in L2 word segmentation. Younger and older L1Spanish-L2Basque bilinguals (n = 158) varying across the four dimensions of interest and a control group of L1Basque bilinguals (n = 63) were tested on a phoneme localization task in Basque. Age did not affect word segmentation in either group. Proficiency modulated performance of the L2Basque bilinguals, with the greatest accuracy gains in sentences containing all sources of information, followed by sentences containing only morphosyntactic and phonological cues, then sentences comprising only phonological information. Frequency of language switch and fluid intelligence were associated with better overall performance, though their contribution to explaining the variance was very small. Finally, natives benefited more than non-natives from lexico-semantic cues, and from morphosyntactic and phonological cues for word-initial targets. These findings suggest the stability of segmentation abilities across the adult lifespan, and evidence how different bilingual factors shape multiple cue use in L2 segmentation.

papers.title: Isolating task-related, low-level, and high-level influences on interobserver congruency of eye movements in scene viewing
papers.authors: Marek A. Pedziwiatr, Sophie Heer, Kristina Zeljic et al.
papers.summary: Why do different people look at similar places in the same image? The researchers picked images where visual clutter and semantic complexity (measured with a distributional semantic model) were uncorrelated. Observers either freely viewed them or memorised them, and similarity in gaze was scored with four metrics. Purely spatial similarity dropped with clutter and nothing else, while the two metrics that also track fixation order responded to both clutter and semantic complexity, in opposite directions depending on whether the metric was sensitive to objects. Memorising made viewing more exploratory, which affected only the order-sensitive metrics.
papers.abstract: When different individuals view the same image, their eye movements are often similar. The degree of this similarity is called interobserver congruency (IOC). We investigated how IOC is determined by three factors that impact gaze control: the visual features of an image, its semantic content, and the task observers perform when viewing it. We first quantified the low-level physical features and semantic complexity of images using a well-established measure of visual clutter and a novel measure based on a distributional semantic model, respectively. Then, we selected an image set in which these two measures were uncorrelated and used it in an eye-tracking experiment, in which observers either freely viewed the images or memorised their content. We assessed IOC using four metrics: two capturing purely spatial IOC and two sensitive to spatiotemporal IOC, i.e., considering both the locations and order of fixations. The values of the two spatial metrics decreased with increasing clutter and remained insensitive to the remaining factors we investigated. The two spatiotemporal metrics were sensitive to both clutter and semantic complexity, but, interestingly, in different ways. Specifically, according to a metric that was insensitive to the presence of objects in images, IOC decreased with clutter and increased with semantic complexity, while the metric sensitive to objects showed the opposite pattern. Additionally, we found that the memorization task rendered oculomotor behaviour more exploratory, which had modulatory effects on spatiotemporal - but not spatial - IOC. Together, our findings reveal how factors known to shape gaze behaviour determine IOC.

papers.title: Do bilinguals avoid ambiguity or minimize processing effort? Insights from an online eye-tracking study in spoken Mandarin
papers.authors: Yajun Liu, Antonella Sorace, Kenny Smith
papers.summary: Bilingual speakers often choose more explicit referring forms, so this team asked whether they also avoid lexical ambiguity when naming pictures in spoken Mandarin. Mandarin-English bilinguals in the UK were actually more likely than more-monolingual speakers in China to use an ambiguous label when the context was ambiguous. Online eye-tracking (WebGazer) showed bilinguals looking early at pairs with easy shared labels, while the other group monitored ambiguity depending on what they ended up saying. The pattern fits the idea that bilinguals skip the extra effort of avoiding ambiguity when it's costly, not that they generally tolerate it.
papers.abstract: Previous research on anaphoric reference shows that bilinguals tend to choose more explicit referential forms (e.g., overt pronouns over null pronouns) compared to monolingual speakers. It remains unclear whether this tendency towards greater explicitness extends to other forms of referential uncertainty, such as lexical ambiguity, or whether it depends on specific processing demands of anaphoric reference tasks. Avoiding lexical ambiguity may be demanding because it requires speakers to inhibit a readily accessible shared (ambiguous) label and retrieve a less accessible, more specific alternative. By conducting two experiments examining lexical ambiguity in spoken Mandarin, we tested two hypotheses: Hypothesis 1 : bilinguals would rather be redundant than ambiguous in general; Hypothesis 2 : bilinguals are less likely to avoid ambiguity when doing so is too costly. In Experiment 1, L1 Mandarin L2 English speakers in the UK and more-monolingual speakers in China completed a picture naming task. We manipulated whether the preferred label was ambiguous in the visual context (Ambiguous Condition) or unambiguous (Unambiguous Condition) and tested whether speakers avoided ambiguous labels. Experiment 2 extended this task by incorporating online eye-tracking using WebGazer. Our results showed that, contrary to Hypothesis 1 , bilinguals were more likely than more-monolinguals to use ambiguous expressions for ambiguous trials. Eye-tracking analysis revealed that bilinguals tended to direct early attention towards image pairs with more accessible shared labels, indicating a preference for linguistic choices that are cognitively less demanding; by contrast, more-monolinguals showed proactive monitoring of ambiguity depending on their responses. These findings support Hypothesis 2 , suggesting that bilingual referential choices may be shaped by domain-specific processing demands rather than by a general preference for avoiding ambiguity. These findings also shed light on cognitive constraints in bilingual lexical access and early signs of lexical attrition.

papers.title: Reading longer does not help: Reaction times predict general comprehension but not garden-path recovery
papers.authors: Markéta Ceháková, Jan Chromý
papers.summary: Slower reading at the disambiguating point of a garden-path sentence is often taken as a sign of effortful repair. In a self-paced reading study, the researchers checked whether longer reading times predicted correct interpretations on comprehension questions. They didn't: for garden-path sentences, reading time had no effect on recovering the right analysis or dropping the wrong one, though slower reading did help for unambiguous sentences. So recovery looks like all-or-nothing, depending on whether readers find a workable alternative rather than how long they spend.
papers.abstract: Comprehenders often retain incorrect interpretations of garden-path sentences, suggesting that sentence representations are not always fully revised after misanalysis. A common assumption is that the additional processing time observed at disambiguation reflects effortful syntactic repair and should therefore improve final interpretations. We tested this prediction by examining whether reaction times predict successful recovery from misanalysis. Participants read ambiguous and unambiguous sentences in a self-paced reading task and answered comprehension questions probing four components of interpretation: inhibition of the initial misanalysis of the ambiguous region, finding the correct interpretation of the ambiguous region, and correct and incorrect interpretations of the disambiguating region. RTs were analyzed at the disambiguating, spillover, and sentence-final regions. Garden-path sentences produced robust processing slowdowns and reduced comprehension accuracy. However, longer RTs did not increase the likelihood of obtaining the correct interpretation. Slower reading improved accuracy for unambiguous sentences, but it had no effect in garden-path sentences. The same pattern (with the effect being present in the unambiguous, but not in the ambiguous condition) was found even in sentence regions unrelated to reanalysis. Critically, for the correct interpretation of the ambiguous region and the inhibition of the initial misanalysis, processing time had no effect in garden-path sentences: readers either recovered the intended analysis or retained a misinterpretation regardless of how long they processed the input. These findings challenge the assumption that processing slowdowns index successful syntactic revision and instead suggest that reanalysis outcomes are largely time-independent, reflecting whether a viable alternative interpretation is found rather than how long readers process the disambiguating input.

papers.title: Subjective equality of visual self-motion and walking speed in virtual environments depends on the field of view
papers.authors: Patricia R. Mueller, Wolfgang Einhäuser
papers.summary: Participants walked on a treadmill in front of a panoramic screen showing a street scene, then adjusted the scene's speed until it felt like it matched their walking speed. Only parts of the visual field showed motion, which let the researchers see how much each region mattered. The central visual field had to move noticeably faster than the walker's real speed to feel right, with a lower gain needed in equally sized peripheral regions. Step length explained some of the large individual differences, though body height and leg length didn't. The results matter for designing VR setups with a limited field of view.
papers.abstract: Typical visual displays cover only a fraction of the visual field. How do such restrictions influence the perception of visual speed during self-motion? While surrounded by a panoramic screen on which an alley of terraced houses was presented, participants walked at constant speed on a treadmill. They adjusted the speed of the visual scene to match their subjectively experienced walking speed. We manipulated which areas of the visual field remained visible. Only this effective Field of View (FoV) contributed to stimulation by scene motion, while the remainder of the scene was replaced by a homogenous grey overlay with no optic flow. We found that the central part of the visual field needs to be presented substantially faster than the actual walking speed to be perceived as matching. This ratio of visual to actual walking speed ("gain") is lower for equally sized parts of the visual periphery. This result is mainly explained by motion-energy density, but there are also unique contributions of size and position in the visual field (including interaction of the three). There is substantial inter-individual variability in the overall gain perceived as optimal, which is in part explained by step length, but shows no relation to anthropometric measures (body height, leg length). Our results quantify the contribution of different visual field areas to motion perception in complex scenes and are of specific relevance for simulating self-motion, especially in virtual-reality setups with limited horizontal FoV.

papers.title: Naturally disengaging control to reveal habits.
papers.authors: Sarah Oh, Anne G. E. Collins
papers.summary: Habits are hard to catch in the lab because people tend to use goal-directed control. Instead of forcing fast responses, this team built a short task that encourages people to relax control on their own, using multistep trials, chances to self-correct, and frequent switching between heavily and lightly practiced behaviors. Across seven experiments, overtraining increased slips of action toward the heavily practiced context in early responses, while slower responses stayed goal-directed. Allowing multiple response attempts was especially important for seeing the effect, and the role of hierarchical structure stayed unclear.
papers.abstract: Habits are an essential part of everyday decision making, yet the mechanisms underlying human habit formation and expression are difficult to study in laboratory settings, where participants typically engage strong goal-directed (GD) control that can mask habitual tendencies. Recent approaches have successfully elicited habits in long experiments by limiting the amount of GD control participants can exert (e.g., through forced response times). We extend this approach by designing a short behavioral paradigm that aims to induce and reveal habits without extrinsically limiting GD control, instead incorporating task features that we hypothesized would encourage participants to spontaneously relax GD control: a hierarchical multistep trial structure, opportunities for self-correction, and frequent switches between extensively and minimally practiced behaviors. Across seven experiments, we demonstrate that this approach induces habitual control in a relatively brief paradigm. Specifically, overtraining increases slips of action toward the extensively practiced context and reduces slips toward the minimally practiced one, indicating behavioral inflexibility at early response times, while slower responses remain dominated by GD control. Systematic manipulation of task features across experiments revealed that allowing multiple response attempts was particularly important for reliably observing this overtraining effect; a hierarchical trial structure may further facilitate habit expression, though this remains inconclusive. More broadly, our paradigm provides a practical tool for investigating how habits form and interact with goal-directed control. (PsycInfo Database Record (c) 2026 APA, all rights reserved).

papers.title: Control dilemmas exist on different levels of information processing: Flexibility and stability trade off at the task level.
papers.authors: Andrea Janker, Sebastian Musslick, Gesine Dreisbach
papers.summary: The classic idea is that staying focused (stability) and switching tasks (flexibility) trade off, but recent work has questioned it. This paper suggests the trade-off may only show up within the same level of processing. In three task-switching experiments with distractors, people were shielded from distractors belonging to the other task when the interference was at the task level. At the stimulus level, that shielding was bypassed, probably by learned stimulus-response associations. Shielding against the other task on one trial hurt performance when the task then switched, supporting a trade-off at the task level.
papers.abstract: Our cognitive system must manage two opposing demands: staying focused on one task (stability) and switching between tasks when needed (flexibility). Traditionally, a trade-off has been assumed between these two control modes. Recent studies questioned this idea. However, they do not consider that experimental manipulations can influence stability and flexibility at different levels of information processing and that a trade-off may only exist within the same level. We introduce a novel paradigm designed to investigate flexibility and stability at different levels of information processing (task vs. stimulus level). Participants switched between two categorization tasks while ignoring distractors. Distractors either came from the same (within-task) or the alternative task (between-task) and were either response congruent or incongruent. In Experiments 1 and 2, participants categorized words superimposed on distractor images representing the generic response categories (task-level interference). In Experiment 3, they categorized letters or digits flanked by distractor letters or digits (stimulus-level interference). Reduced interference from between-task distractors compared with within-task distractors in Experiments 1 and 2 show shielding at the task level. At the stimulus level (Experiment 3), both distractor types interfered to the same extent, indicating that the shielding against between-task distractors got bypassed by the automatic retrieval of learned stimulus-response associations. Across all three experiments, shielding against between-task distractors in the previous trial impaired performance, when the task switched (i.e., it impaired flexibility). This finding supports a trade-off between flexibility and stability at the task level. (PsycInfo Database Record (c) 2026 APA, all rights reserved).

papers.title: From simulation to reality: Empirical validation of the superiority of da in indexing sensitivity in recognition-memory experiments.
papers.authors: Adva Levi, Caren M. Rotello, Yonatan Goshen-Gottstein
papers.summary: Many sensitivity measures for yes/no recognition data get mixed up with response bias, and earlier simulations from this lab suggested only their confidence-rating-based da avoids that. Here they tested it in two large recognition experiments where sensitivity was held equal and only bias varied at test. Using resampling, only da produced false positives at the expected 5% rate, while Pr, A′ and d′ didn't, and da's power to detect real differences was comparable to the others. The data sets are openly available.
papers.abstract: The selection of an accuracy (sensitivity) measure is a pivotal decision faced by researchers who use binary judgments.An abundance of measures has been developed to index sensitivity independent of participants' bias.However, recent Monte Carlo simulations ran in our lab found that all commonly used measures confound sensitivity with bias, with the exception of our proposed version of the signal-detection measure d-sub-a (denoted d a ), based on confidence ratings rather than binary responses.Nevertheless, empirical confirmation in real-world experiments is needed to validate any measure.To this end, we ran two large-scale recognition studies that can serve as a proof of concept to all binary tasks.Sensitivity was not manipulated at encoding, while we manipulated bias at test.When comparing these iso-sensitive conditions, valid measures should yield erroneous significant results at approximately 5% (or α).Using resampling, we repeatedly ran the experiment to derive rates of Type-I errors.Only d a , but not P r , A′, or d′, demonstrated the desired 5% rate of Type-I errors across different experimental designs, sample sizes, and number of trials.We also used our data to assess statistical power.We compared d a 's ability to detect genuine sensitivity differences and found detection rates similar to all other measures tested.Combined with our simulation results, these empirical findings provide compelling evidence that d a is a valid and powerful sensitivity measure.Our findings offer a validated measure that can reduce the hazards of the measurement crisis that plague recognition-memory research.Our large data sets, available online, provide opportunities for future analyses.

papers.title: The transposed-word effect persists across text orientations in Chinese
papers.authors: Yuru Cheng, Kuo Zhang, Zhiwei Liu et al.
papers.summary: In grammaticality judgments, swapped-word sequences are harder to reject than they should be, which suggests readers process word order flexibly. Two hundred native Chinese readers judged five-word sequences shown left-to-right, top-to-bottom, right-to-left, or bottom-to-top. The transposed-word effect showed up in accuracy and reaction times in every orientation, but it was biggest for conventional left-to-right text. Since all words were visible at once, the shrinkage can't just be blamed on serial presentation. It could reflect more serial word recognition or narrower attention and less parafoveal uptake, so the results fit both accounts.
papers.abstract: In speeded grammaticality decision tasks, the transposed-word effect occurs when ungrammatical word sequences created by swapping adjacent words in an otherwise grammatical sentence are harder to reject than control sequences derived from ungrammatical base sentences, providing evidence for flexible word-order processing during reading. Previous research shows that this effect is often attenuated in atypical display formats, including serial word presentation and backward text, especially in RTs. Some accounts interpret this pattern as a shift from parallel processing, in which multiple words are recognised simultaneously, towards more serial word recognition. However, atypical formats may also disrupt component processes supporting reading, including eye guidance, spatial attention, and parafoveal processing, thereby reducing the uptake of information from adjacent words. We extended this work to Chinese, a script that can be read in horizontal and vertical orientations while individual characters remain upright. Two hundred native Chinese readers made speeded grammaticality decisions to five-word sequences presented left-to-right, top-to-bottom, right-to-left, or bottom-to-top. Robust transposed-word effects occurred in both accuracy and RTs across all orientations. Effects were largest for conventional left-to-right text and smaller in all three atypical orientations. Thus, attenuation occurred even though all words remained simultaneously visible. It was therefore not confined to formats that physically enforce serial presentation. Although attenuation may reflect a shift towards more serial word recognition, it could also arise because difficulty processing atypically oriented text narrows spatial attention and reduces parafoveal information uptake. These component-process changes can occur under either parallel or serial accounts, making the findings compatible with both.

papers.title: The effect of the spatial distribution of attention on the perception of apparent motion
papers.authors: Fuminori Ono
papers.summary: A motion quartet is an ambiguous display that can look like horizontal or vertical motion. Across three experiments, the researchers shifted attention along one axis, either with elongated cues or with a secondary task that controlled for the cues' physical properties. Whatever the method, people tended to see motion along the attended axis, horizontal when attention was horizontal and vertical when vertical. This suggests how attention is spread across space plays a real role in deciding how moving elements get matched up.
papers.abstract: Apparent motion perception depends on both stimulus properties and attentional allocation, yet the role of the spatial distribution of attention remains unclear. The present study examined whether biases in attentional distribution systematically modulate bistable apparent motion perception. Using a motion quartet stimulus, three experiments manipulated attention along horizontal and vertical axes. In Experiments 1 and 2, attention was biased using elongated attentional cues. In Experiment 3, attention was manipulated via a secondary task while controlling for physical cue properties. Across all experiments, perceived motion direction was biased toward the attended axis: horizontal motion predominated under horizontal attention, whereas vertical motion predominated under vertical attention. These results demonstrate that the spatial distribution of attention plays a functional role in motion correspondence and highlight attention as a key factor shaping apparent motion perception.

papers.title: Boundary memory and image memorability are systematically related
papers.authors: Yongseong Lee, Su Keun Jeong
papers.summary: People tend to remember scenes as extending further than they really did (boundary extension), and some images are consistently more memorable than others. This team asked whether the two are linked. Images with more boundary extension had higher memorability, both when comparing an existing dataset to deep-learning memorability predictions and in new behavioral experiments with recognition tests. Manipulations known to boost boundary extension also raised predicted memorability, which hints at shared image properties behind both effects.
papers.abstract: Boundary extension refers to the tendency to remember scenes as having wider boundaries than were physically present. A separate line of research has shown that image memorability, defined as the likelihood that an image will be remembered across observers, varies substantially across images. Previous research suggests that both boundary extension and image memorability heavily depend on image characteristics, yet the possibility that the two phenomena are related has not been directly tested. In the current study, we asked whether images that produce stronger boundary extension also tend to be more memorable. First, we compared boundary transformation scores from an existing dataset with memorability estimates generated by a deep-learning model. Results revealed that images showing greater boundary extension tended to have higher predicted memorability. Next, we conducted behavioral experiments measuring boundary memory for scene images and directly assessed recognition memory for the same images. Consistent with the first analysis, images associated with greater boundary extension showed higher memorability. Finally, analyses of experimentally manipulated stimuli showed that image manipulations known to increase boundary extension also increased predicted memorability. Taken together, these findings reveal a systematic relationship between boundary memory and memorability, suggesting that shared image properties may influence both the tendency to extend scene boundaries and the strength of memory encoding.

papers.title: Lapses of attention
papers.authors: Nash Unsworth
papers.summary: This review covers attention lapses: the different types, how they're measured, and their neural and physiological correlates. It proposes a general resource-allocation framework to explain what drives lapses, including arousal, distraction, worries, motivation, task demands and individual differences. It also looks at knock-on effects on selective attention, working memory, learning, reading comprehension and error monitoring, as well as lapses in everyday life, and argues for tighter definitions and theories and more work on reducing lapses.
papers.abstract: The literature on lapses of attention is organized and reviewed. This includes a review of different types of lapses, different measures of lapses, and neural and physiological correlates of lapses. A general attention resource-allocation framework is proposed to explain lapses and what factors influence their occurrence. These factors include arousal/alertness, external distraction, personal concerns and negative thoughts, motivational/conative factors, task factors, and person factors. Research is reviewed suggesting that lapses have downstream effects on a number of processes including selective attention and attention control, working memory, learning, reading comprehension, and error monitoring. Finally, lapses in everyday life are reviewed. A number of future directions are discussed and it is suggested that more research is needed to refine our definition and theories of lapses and examine additional ways of curtailing lapses.

papers.title: The temporal dynamics of semantic guidance in scenes
papers.authors: Taylor R. Hayes, John M. Henderson
papers.summary: One hundred people viewed one hundred real-world scenes, and the researchers modeled four semantic features at each location to see how they guided where people looked over time. Similarity to the scene category and local semantic intensity predicted early fixations but faded, while a preference for semantically distinctive objects stayed steady. Similarity to the last-fixated object reversed, with related regions under-selected early and over-selected later. The authors read this as a shift from seeking novel information to integrating related content, with several semantic processes running in parallel and changing in weight.
papers.abstract: When viewing a complex scene, the visual system must decide where to look among many potential targets. How this selection process unfolds over time-and whether it reflects changing semantic priorities-remains poorly understood. We tracked eye movements of 100 participants viewing 100 real-world scenes and modeled four distinct semantic features at each location: similarity to the scene category, similarity to other objects, similarity to the most recently fixated object, and local semantic intensity. Complementary Bayesian models of fixation likelihood and fixation onset time revealed that each feature follows a distinct temporal trajectory. Scene-category similarity and semantic intensity strongly predicted early fixations but weakened over time, consistent with rapid gist-derived guidance. Preference for semantically distinctive objects remained stable throughout viewing. Similarity to the previously fixated object showed a temporal reversal: relative to each scanpath's own baseline, semantically related regions were under-selected early and over-selected later. These dynamics were robust to controls for central viewing bias and distance to the previous fixation, ruling out purely spatial or oculomotor explanations. Together, these patterns suggest a shift from information maximization early in viewing, when attention prioritizes novel, non-redundant semantic content, to conceptual integration later, when attention is increasingly directed to semantically related elements. Rather than discrete processing stages, multiple semantic processes appear to operate in parallel with shifting weights over time, revealing how stored knowledge is associated with attention in complex scenes. OPEN PRACTICES STATEMENT: The scene stimuli, fixation data, semantic feature maps, fitted model outputs, and analysis code for reproducing all results are available on the Open Science Framework: https://osf.io/7uspw . This study was not preregistered.

papers.title: Estimating stimulus-processing time via position slopes in visual search
papers.authors: Talke Michaelsen, Markus Janczyk, Heinrich R. Liesefeld
papers.summary: Measuring how long it takes to process a single stimulus is tricky, since response time mixes in other things like response initiation, and ordinary set-size slopes assume you know how many items were actually processed. The systematic-search paradigm gets around this by controlling search order, so target position tells you how many items were processed, and the slope relating position to response time estimates processing time per stimulus. Two preregistered experiments further validated it: the slope reflected how complex the visual stimuli were but didn't change when the response got more complex.
papers.abstract: Existing approaches to measure the time needed to process a single stimulus have confounded the measure with other time-consuming processes, such as initiation of the response, and neglect the massively parallel processing abilities of the visual system. Conversely, traditional set-size manipulations in visual search yield flawed estimates of stimulus-processing time, mainly because the number of actually processed stimuli is typically unknown. We have recently developed the systematic-search paradigm , a visual-search paradigm that overcomes this limitation and potentially provides a valid measure of stimulus-processing time. Its core idea is to bring the order of search under experimental control, so that the number of processed stimuli is determined by the position of the target on the current trial. We then extract the slope of the linear function relating target position (and therefore the number of processed stimuli) to response times. With this approach, all extraneous processing times are relegated to the intercept of the function. The present study provides a further validation of this slope-measure by showing that it reflects the complexity of the visual stimuli (Exp. 1), but is robust against changes in the complexity of the response (Exp. 2). All raw data, analysis code, preregistrations, and research materials are available online ( https://osf.io/42mxh/ ). Open practices statement In both experiments, we report how we determined our sample size, all data exclusions (if any), all manipulations, and all measures in the study. The experiments’ designs and analyses were preregistered. All trial-level raw data, analysis code, preregistrations and research materials are available online ( https://osf.io/42mxh/ ). Direct links to the preregistrations are https://osf.io/tbk8s/ (Exp. 1) and https://osf.io/va98q/ (Exp. 2).

papers.title: Can bilingual readers process language membership of multiple words in parallel?
papers.authors: Aybora Koc, Agnesa Xheladini, Mathieu Declerck
papers.summary: Can bilingual readers pick up which language several words belong to all at once? Dutch-English bilinguals did a lexical decision task with flanking words, shown for either 50 ms (too short to read sequentially) or 170 ms. They were slower on the target when the flankers were in the other language, but only at 170 ms; the effect disappeared at 50 ms. That points to only limited parallel extraction of language membership across words.
papers.abstract: We examined whether bilingual readers can extract language membership information from multiple words at once. Dutch-English bilinguals completed a lexical decision task in a flankers paradigm, with viewing times manipulated either to constrain (50 ms) or allow (170 ms) sequential reading. The findings revealed reliable congruency effects (i.e., slower on the central target word when the flankers were presented in a different language than when they were presented in the same language) in 170 ms, but this effect disappeared when the stimulus was presented for 50 ms. The pattern indicates limited parallel extraction of language membership information across multiple words. OPEN PRACTICES STATEMENT: The data that support the findings of this study are openly available in OSF ( https://doi.org/10.17605/OSF.IO/MX2NU ). The stimuli, trial-level data for both experiments, and the analysis code are provided in this repository link. The study was not preregistered.

papers.title: Object speed and distractor number affect performance but not attentional allocation in multiple object tracking
papers.authors: N. Adamian, F. Akalan, S. K.Andersen
papers.summary: Faster objects and more distractors make multiple object tracking harder, but does that happen because attention to each target gets weaker, as it does when you add targets? In two EEG experiments (70 people total), tracking accuracy dropped as speed and object number increased. However, steady-state visual evoked potentials showed that attentional enhancement of targets over distractors didn't decline. The authors conclude that bottom-up display demands and top-down attention affect tracking independently, and that attention allocation seems driven by goals rather than display characteristics.
papers.abstract: Keeping track of multiple moving objects across dynamic real-world scenarios such as driving, team sports, or crowded social environments is a fundamental challenge for visual attention. We have previously demonstrated that as the number of tracked objects increases, the strength of attentional facilitation allocated to each individual object decreases, limiting tracking success. It is also well established that beyond the number of tracked objects, faster-moving objects and objects embedded amongst higher numbers of distractors are more difficult to track. Are these effects on tracking difficulty also mediated by less effective allocation of attention to tracked targets as in the case of tracking more targets? If so, one should expect the strength of attentional modulation to drop systematically with increasing speed and total number of moving stimuli. In two experiments (total n = 70), participants were instructed to track moving targets amongst identical distractors while we manipulated object speed (Experiment 1) and number (Experiment 2). As expected, tracking performance declined with both manipulations. However, steady-state visual evoked potentials (SSVEPs) recorded during successful tracking revealed that attentional enhancement of tracked targets compared with distractors did not drop with increasing speed or object number. In summary, bottom-up changes in the stimulus display and top-down attentional manipulations affect tracking performance in independent ways, with the balance between strength of attentional allocation and bottom-up demands of the task determining successful tracking. The allocation of attention itself seems to be determined exclusively by top-down goals rather than being reactive to bottom-up display characteristics. Significance statement Keeping track of multiple moving objects is fundamental to navigating dynamic real-world scenarios. This ability is accomplished through multifocal attentional selection, which weakens as the number of tracked targets increases. This study asks whether other stimulus manipulations increase tracking difficulty by diluting attentional allocation. Using steady-state visual evoked potentials to measure selective attention during tracking, we demonstrate that both increases in speed and distractor number impair performance, but they do not affect attentional enhancement of targets relative to distractors. This suggests that top-down attentional control operates independently from bottom-up demands.

papers.title: Artists Can Design Memory, and AI Can Predict It
papers.authors: Trent M. Davis, Yifei E. Chen, Wilma A. Bainbridge
papers.summary: Artists entered a nationwide contest with works meant to be either memorable or forgettable, and recognition tasks with a few hundred to a thousand online and gallery participants showed they mostly hit their targets. The effect was lopsided, though: making art memorable was easier than making it forgettable. A neural network called ResMem predicted which works would stick better than people or the artists themselves, and the features that explained nearly half the variance in memory lined up with ResMem's predictions but not with human judgments.
papers.abstract: Can artists deliberately design artworks to be remembered—or forgotten? Across three experiments, we tested whether visual-memory outcomes can be shaped through artistic design and how they are predicted by artists, laypeople, and artificial intelligence. We launched a nationwide art contest in which artists submitted works intended to be memorable or forgettable. Using recognition tasks with adults based in the United States (119 from Amazon Mechanical Turk, 892 from Prolific, and 62 visitors from a Chicago gallery), we found that artists achieved their intended memory outcomes. However, their success was asymmetric: Memorability was more readily increased than reduced. A neural network, ResMem, consistently outperformed human observers and artists in predicting which artworks would be remembered. Data-driven analyses identified psychologically interpretable features that explained nearly half the variance in memory and aligned with ResMem’s predictions, but not with human judgments. Together, findings suggest that visual memorability can be engineered by humans, though asymmetrically, and is better captured by computational models.

papers.title: Trait judgements of faces using a task without word labels
papers.authors: Yue Xu, Umit Keles, Chujun Lin et al.
papers.summary: Instead of giving people trait words like 'trustworthy' to rate, over 3,000 participants simply arranged unfamiliar faces in space by how similar the people seemed. The first experiment produced five dimensions (approachability, gender-specific warmth, competence, morality, youthfulness), and a second with White, Black and Asian faces also gave five, with clear race-stereotype effects. Comparing this with word-label studies, the authors argue that approachability or warmth acts as a universal, holistic evaluative factor, while race and gender stereotypes depend on which faces are shown.
papers.abstract: People attribute psychological traits to faces. Previous research has typically elicited these judgements using specific words provided in advance by the experimenter (for example, ratings on competence or trustworthiness), raising questions about completeness (these tasks use a limited set of words) and generalizability (for example, across languages). Here we asked over 3,000 participants to spatially arrange unfamiliar faces based on perceived trait similarity, without providing any word labels. Using predominantly White faces, experiment 1 yielded five dimensions that we interpreted as approachability, gender-specific warmth, competence, morality and youthfulness. Using White, Black and Asian faces, experiment 2 also produced five dimensions, which showed prominent effects of stereotypes associated with race. Comparisons with four other studies that used word labels argue that approachability or warmth emerges as a universal evaluative factor that integrates multiple trait facets (such as trustworthiness, warmth and competence) into a single holistic dimension and that race and gender stereotypes emerge depending on the set of face stimuli used.

papers.title: Is there a neural common factor for visual illusions?
papers.authors: Maya A. Jastrzębowska, Ayberk Ozkirli, Aline F. Cretenoud et al.
papers.summary: Earlier work reported that the surface area of primary visual cortex (V1) predicts how susceptible people are to several spatial illusions, which is puzzling since illusions barely correlate with each other in behavior. Here the researchers tried to re-evaluate those imaging results and extended the test to more illusions. They couldn't replicate the earlier finding and found no other significant correlations, either between illusions or between illusion susceptibility and visual neuroanatomy.
papers.abstract: It has been reported that the surface area of the human primary visual cortex predicts the susceptibility to several spatial contextual illusions. Yet, contrary to common belief, illusions correlate only weakly at the perceptual level, raising the question of how they can correlate with a neural measure like V1 surface area. In addition, mounting evidence suggests that there is substantial interindividual variability not only in neural function and anatomy but also in the mapping between the two, which further challenges the findings of a neural common factor for illusions. In light of these concerns, our first goal was to re-evaluate the previous imaging results. Seeking to investigate whether these findings generalize, we expanded our study to other illusions. We could not replicate previous findings and did not find any other significant correlations, either at the perceptual level or between illusion susceptibility and visual functional neuroanatomy.

papers.title: Decoding object categories from electroencephalography during free viewing reveals early information evolution compared to passive viewing
papers.authors: Carmel R. Auerbach-Asch, Gal Vishne, Oded Wertheimer et al.
papers.summary: EEG decoding studies usually have people hold their eyes still while images flash up, which is a bit unlike real vision. Here the researchers used a deconvolution method to untangle overlapping brain responses and decoded object categories from single fixations during free viewing, then compared this with rapid passive viewing. Category information could be decoded in both, the representations generalized across them, and the signal time-locked to fixation appeared earlier than the one time-locked to stimulus onset, which hints that object processing starts parafoveally, around the time of the saccade.
papers.abstract: Object processing is central to visual perception, and its neural substrates inform cognitive and computational models of vision. Electroencephalographic (EEG) research has increasingly adopted multivariate pattern analysis (MVPA) to decode distributed neural representations, moving beyond average signal changes and predefined electrodes. Yet, most MVPA studies use passive viewing paradigms that constrain eye movements and evoke brain activity by external stimuli presentation, creating an artificial dissociation between perception and action. Here, we examine object category representations during active vision by combining MVPA with a deconvolution method for overlapping fixation-related responses. By decoding category information from single fixations, we compare the temporal dynamics of object processing between free viewing (active) and rapid serial visual presentation (passive) conditions.
