We find that categorical information, across multiple levels of abstraction, can be decoded from individual fixations during natural viewing, and that object representations generalize across passive and active conditions. Notably, representational dynamics time-locked to fixation onset emerge earlier than those time-locked to stimulus onset. We discuss the possibility that object processing begins parafoveally, aligned with saccade onset, rather than foveally at fixation. Thus, information about what and when to expect new information, available in free viewing, facilitates processing. These findings underscore the importance of studying vision in naturalistic settings and highlight key methodological considerations for combining MVPA with deconvolution in overlapping neural data. Object processing is fundamental to visual perception and to cognitive and computational models of vision. Although MVPA has advanced EEG research by enabling the decoding of distributed neural representations with high temporal precision, it has been applied primarily in passive viewing paradigms that constrain natural eye movements. The current study bridges the gap between passive and active vision research by combining MVPA with overlap deconvolution to decode object category information from EEG during natural fixations in free viewing. This approach reveals that category-specific representations emerge earlier in active viewing, likely reflecting processing that begins during saccade planning or execution. The findings underscore the importance of studying vision under ecologically valid conditions and introduce a novel methodological framework for capturing neural dynamics during active perception.

papers.title: Deep LLM layers expose passage-level context in EEG during silent reading
papers.authors: Ingo Marquardt, Anthilia Alchanat, Priyanka Jain
papers.summary: Building on earlier work decoding words from 19-channel EEG during silent reading, the researchers trained a separate decoder for each of the 33 layers of Llama-3.1-8B. Word-level decodability peaked in early layers and faded toward the end, while the part of the signal that tracks the passage's context grew with depth, even when a decoder only saw a single 0.5-second EEG window. Control analyses suggest this context tracking isn't just a byproduct of word decoding or of session-specific signatures, so the choice of target layer matters for EEG language decoders.
papers.abstract: In a previous report we showed that a decoder can recover open-vocabulary word-level information from 19-channel EEG recorded during silent reading, by aligning short EEG windows with hidden-state embeddings of the presented word taken from a large language model (LLM). That analysis contrasted two of the model's 33 layers: the context-free input embedding and one mid-depth layer. Here we ask how EEG-decodable structure is distributed over the full depth of the language model. We trained one decoder per layer of Llama-3.1-8B, with and without a causal transformer over the sequence of EEG windows. We distinguish word-level decodability from a context-tracking component. Word-level decodability peaks in early layers and declines steadily towards the last layer. In contrast, the context-tracking component of the retrieval gain rises with depth, both with and without a causal transformer. Unexpectedly, a decoder that sees a single 0.5-s window at a time tracks the text passage too. Two new controls dissect this component. A target-geometry control, a synthetic predictor made of the true target plus noise calibrated to each decoder's word-level accuracy, shows that context tracking is not a by-product of word decoding and target geometry. A control that permutes predictions across runs from either the same or from different sessions shows that most of the observed context-tracking is not caused by an EEG recording session signature. Instead, context tracking mostly follows the text. A single EEG window therefore carries passage-level information that a contextual target can absorb. The results locate word identity in the early layers of the language model, discourse state in the deeper layers, and make the choice of target layer a design dial for EEG language decoders.

papers.title: Distributional signatures of computation: inferring mechanisms from computation time distributions
papers.authors: Céline van Valkenhoef, Catherine Schuman, Nikolaus Kriegeskorte et al.
papers.summary: The researchers propose inferring how a physical system computes from the distribution of its computation times, much as reaction-time distributions are used in cognitive science. They tested the idea with a scalable visual search task, comparing humans with three models that accumulate evidence in different ways. Scaling of time with problem size looked broadly similar across models and people, but the shape of the time distributions told the models apart, which suggests a way to compare very different computing systems without seeing inside them.
papers.abstract: Computational complexity theory provides a framework for analysing abstract models of computation, whereas computational systems operate as finite physical implementations whose behaviour is shaped by their architecture and physical substrate. In such systems, computational organisation cannot be directly characterised from algorithms or internal representations. Building on the use of reaction time distributions to constrain mechanisms in cognitive science, we introduce an empirical framework for investigating computation in physical systems by inferring computational mechanisms from observable computation time distributions. The framework combines empirical benchmarking, which characterises computational efficiency through the scaling of computation time with problem size, with distributional analysis, which treats computation time distributions as signatures of the stochastic dynamics generated by different computational mechanisms. We demonstrate the framework using a scalable visual search paradigm, comparing human performance with three computational models that employ distinct mechanisms of evidence accumulation. Benchmarking reveals broadly similar scaling behaviour for the models and human observers, whereas distributional analysis distinguishes between these models. We show that computation time distributions provide an empirical level of description linking observable computational behaviour to underlying computational mechanisms. This framework complements computational complexity theory by extending the empirical study of computation from measuring computational performance to characterising computational organisation. It provides an empirical approach for comparing finite computational systems across diverse physical implementations, including biological, classical, neuromorphic, and quantum systems, without requiring access to their internal algorithms or architectures.

papers.title: What Shapes Brain Alignment of Large Language Models during Dialogue? Insights from Language Production and Comprehension
papers.authors: Yuko Nakagi, Yuya Chiba, Yasue Kishino
papers.summary: Most work comparing large language models to the brain looks at passive listening or reading, so here the researchers used fMRI recorded during actual dialogue, where people both speak and listen. Brain alignment differed between production and comprehension, and was strongly tied to the intrinsic dimension of the LLM representations in regions linked to each mode. The contributions of linguistic and communicative features also varied by processing mode, model layer and brain region.
papers.abstract: Brain alignment of large language models (LLMs) offers a way to investigate representational similarities between LLMs and the human brain during language processing. While previous studies have mainly focused on passive language comprehension, little is known about such alignment during dialogue, in which speakers engage in both language production and comprehension. In this study, using fMRI data collected during dialogue, we examine brain alignment during language production and comprehension across LLM layers and brain regions. We assess its association with the intrinsic dimension (ID) of LLM representations and the contributions of several interpretable linguistic and communicative features. Our results reveal distinct patterns of brain alignment between production and comprehension, as well as strong associations with ID in brain regions associated with each processing mode. Furthermore, we show that the contributions of linguistic and communicative features also vary across processing modes, LLM layers, and brain regions.

papers.title: Individual differences in the computational processes that support face recognition
papers.authors: Fournier Raphaël, Paul Downing, Richard Ramsey
papers.summary: With 300 participants doing a face memory task, the researchers fit an evidence-accumulation model to split performance into latent parameters like drift rate (signal quality) and threshold (response caution). People with better face recognition showed greater drift-rate discrimination, for both learned and novel faces, and this held up after accounting for car recognition ability. They were also more cautious in their responses. The effects were modest, but they point to more efficient information extraction and a more careful decision policy as underlying mechanisms.
papers.abstract: Face recognition ability varies substantially across the population, yet the cognitive and computational processes that give rise to this variation remain poorly understood. Here, we combined approaches from experimental, differential and mathematical psychology to test how individual differences in face recognition ability relate to latent parameters of the decision-making processes involved in face recognition. Participants (N = 300) completed a face memory task with learned and novel faces, together with independent measures of face recognition ability (Cambridge Face Memory Test) and general object recognition ability (car recognition). We modelled task performance with an evidence-accumulation model that translates accuracy and response times into latent parameters, including drift rate (the signal-to-noise ratio of the evidence) and threshold (response caution). Higher face recognition ability was associated with greater drift rate discrimination between correct and incorrect response accumulators in the face memory task, for both learned and novel faces and to a similar degree, consistent with expertise effects in other domains. This association remained largely unchanged when accounting for car recognition ability, suggesting that it is at least partly tied to face processing itself. Higher face recognition ability was also associated with greater response caution, which may reflect better calibration to task demands. Although the associations were modest in size, these findings suggest that individual differences in face recognition ability are reflected in distinct computational mechanisms, namely more efficient extraction of information from faces and a more cautious decision policy. This approach enables a more explicit and computational basis for cognitive theories of face recognition to be developed, as well as for testing whether these mechanisms operate similarly across the full spectrum of face recognition abilities.

papers.title: Detecting the “We-Mode” in Observed Interactions: Infants’ Increasing Selectivity to Cues of “Truly” Joint Attention From 9 to 18 Months
papers.authors: Maleen Thiele, Daniel Hanus
papers.summary: Using looking-time with a novelty-preference test, the researchers showed 9-month-olds and 18-month-olds videos of two adults looking at an object, varying whether they looked at each other and whether they did so in sync. The 18-month-olds encoded the object only in the synchronous, looking-at-partner condition, the one that best signals truly joint attention. The 9-month-olds were less picky and encoded objects whenever the adults looked at each other, even without any sharedness, so sensitivity to observed joint attention seems to get more selective during the second year.
papers.abstract: Human social cognition is grounded in “we-mode” interactions, providing a psychological foundation for coordinating attention and knowledge, thereby facilitating human-specific cultural learning. While infants’ sensitivity to interpersonal sharedness is well-documented in participation-based “first-party” interactions, its ontogenetic origins in observed “third-party” settings remain poorly understood. Focusing on joint attention as a foundational mechanism of shared cognition, this study investigated when infants begin to appreciate the “we-dimension” within observed triadic interactions, addressing theoretical debates between leaner and richer accounts of joint attention. In a screen-based object-encoding task, 9-month-old infants and 18-month-old toddlers saw videos of two adults looking at an object. We systematically manipulated (a) partner-directed gaze (looking at partner vs. away) and (b) its temporal alignment (synchronously vs. asynchronously). This allowed us to contrast “truly joint attention” (coordinated mutual awareness, “we-mode”) with “parallel attention” (mere co-orientation) and a novel “social gaze” condition featuring uncoordinated partner-looks without sharedness. Results from a looking-time-based novelty-preference test revealed that 18-month-olds selectively encoded objects only when observing eye contact in the “synchronous–looking at partner” condition, indicative of “truly joint attention”. Conversely, 9-month-olds exhibited a broader sensitivity, encoding objects in all conditions featuring partner-directed gaze, including “social gaze” scenarios lacking markers of sharedness. These findings demonstrate that infants’ early sensitivity to third-party joint attention refines into a more selective appreciation of the observed “we-dimension” during the second year. This developmental progression marks a critical milestone in recognizing others’ collaborative engagement, providing the foundation for the specialized observational learning that underpins human-unique cultural transmission.

papers.title: Valence Automatically Elicits Vowel Articulation
papers.authors: Saru Parajuli, Charlotte Sophie Löffler, Ralf Rummer et al.
papers.summary: People tend to link the vowel /i/ with positive valence and /o/ with more negative, and this study asked whether that link is automatic. Participants (N=47) classified happy and angry faces by saying /i/ or /o/, in blocks where the mapping either matched or opposed that association. They started speaking faster in the congruent blocks, and pitch patterns also differed by congruency and vowel, supporting the idea that vowel-valence associations operate automatically.
papers.abstract: The association between vowels and valence is known as valence sound symbolism. For example, the vowel /i/ (as in English "meet") is associated with more positive valence than the vowel /o/ (as in German “Boot”). The present experiment employs an implicit paradigm to determine whether valence sound symbolism, like size and shape sound symbolism, operates automatically. Participants (N = 47) classified valenced facial expressions by articulating the target vowels /i/ or /o/. Specifically, in the congruent blocks, participants were instructed to say /i/ for happy and /o/ for angry faces, and in the incongruent blocks, to say /i/ for angry and /o/ for happy faces. Response initiation times were faster in congruent compared to incongruent blocks. An additional analysis of acoustic parameters revealed a significant interaction between congruency and vowel type for pitch (f0). Specifically, /i/ was produced with higher pitch in the congruent blocks (happy faces) than in the incongruent blocks (angry faces), whereas /o/ was produced with higher pitch in the incongruent blocks (happy faces) than in the congruent blocks (angry faces). In sum, the present results indicate that the association between vowels and valence operates automatically, thereby contributing to our knowledge of cognitive processing during valence sound symbolism.

papers.title: Investigating the Factors Motivating the Adoption of Optimal Attentional Strategies
papers.authors: Tianyu Zhang, Molly R McKinney, Isaac Savelson et al.
papers.summary: People often don't use the most efficient attentional strategies in visual search, so the researchers tested whether motivation could help, using the Adaptive Choice Visual Search task. Limiting how long search items were visible didn't lead to better strategy choices, but paying more for faster performance produced a modest improvement. The link between motivation and strategy optimization looks real but weak, and finding a stronger boost remains an open problem.
papers.abstract: Our goal-directed attentional control abilities enable us to flexibly maximize how efficiently we search the visual environment. However, a growing body of research reveals that we often fail to use these abilities. Here, we question how motivational incentives might be used to improve attentional control strategies. Using the Adaptive Choice Visual Search (Irons &amp; Leber, 2018), a task designed to measure attentional strategy use, we manipulated motivation in two ways. In Experiment 1, we limited the exposure of the visual search items, and in Experiment 2, we provided a greater monetary reward for faster search performance. In both experiments, we reasoned that participants would choose the search strategies that enabled faster target identification times; faster search would reduce errors in Experiment 1 and increase earnings in Experiment 2. Results showed that the time-pressure manipulation failed to induce more optimal strategy choices, while the performance-contingent reward manipulation did induce a modest improvement in strategy. Overall, we find some evidence of a link between motivation and strategy optimization, although methods to elicit a more robust boost in optimization remain elusive. Further work is needed in this understudied but vital domain of research.

papers.title: Beyond validity: Empirical investigations of the statistical power of da in Recognition Memory
papers.authors: Adva Levi, Caren M. Rotello, Yonatan Goshen-Gottstein
papers.summary: Common sensitivity measures in recognition memory (d′, A′, percent correct, Pr) are confounded with response bias, and da has been proposed as a bias-independent alternative. After earlier work showing it has a low false-discovery rate, this study checked its statistical power by resampling data from 960 online participants who did a recognition task under two sensitivity conditions. da matched the commonly used measures in significance rates, reaching 80% power with about 48 participants, which supports recommending it as the measure of choice.
papers.abstract: Recognition memory relies on sensitivity measures to identify memory effects (i.e., differences in sensitivity). Alas, all commonly used sensitivity measures (d′, A′, Percent correct, and Pr) have been shown to be confounded with response bias, raising serious validity concerns for the literature. da, a signal-detection measure grounded in the Unequal-Variance Signal-Detection model, has been proposed as a bias-independent alternative. Yet, establishing da as the gold standard for measuring memory effects requires demonstrating not only that it produces low rates of false discoveries, but also that it has sufficient statistical power to detect genuine differences in sensitivity. The low false discovery rate has been established with both simulated and large-scale experiments (Levi, Danino, et al., 2026; Levi, Rotello &amp; Goshen-Gottstein, 2026). Here, we examined the estimated power of da using empirical data from 960 online participants who completed a recognition task under two sensitivity conditions (repetition manipulation). We used resampling techniques to test power levels for multiple sample sizes and found that da achieved significance rates comparable to those of the commonly-used measures, regardless of the statistical test or effect size. The typical 80% power threshold was achieved with approximately 48 participants. Together with our previous findings, these results establish da as a valid and statistically powerful measure, thus confirming the recommendation to adopt da as the measure of choice in recognition memory research.

papers.title: Similarity Judgments Reveal the Multidimensional Representations of Naturalistic Faces
papers.authors: Natalie Peluso, Amanda K Robinson, Tijl Grootswagers et al.
papers.summary: Most face perception research uses posed, controlled images, so here 365 adults aged 20 to 76 judged similarity among 75 naturalistic face photos. Smiling faces clustered together regardless of gender and age, while non-smiling adult faces sorted by apparent gender. Multidimensional scaling and representational similarity analysis showed that perceptual organization followed physical attributes like facial action units and age more than social inferences or classic emotion categories.
papers.abstract: The human face affords a remarkable array of complex social cues, yet our understanding of how it is spontaneously perceived relies almost exclusively on controlled, posed stimuli that suppress the natural variation which makes faces so informative. Here, using a data-driven similarity task with 75 naturalistic face images, we mapped perceptual judgments across 365 adults aged 20 to 76. The results indicated that naturalistic face space was hierarchically organized by physical and demographic cues: smiling faces formed a coherent category that transcended gender and age, whereas non-smiling adult faces stratified along apparent gender. Multidimensional scaling and representational similarity analysis revealed that perceptual organization was driven by physical attributes – including facial action unit and age – rather than higher order social inferences or classic emotion categories. These findings reveal a robust, flexible geometry that accommodates naturalistic facial variation, advancing a more ecologically valid framework for real-world social perception.

papers.title: Apathy is associated with lower perceptual curiosity
papers.authors: Leon Tay, Patrick Cooper, Emily Colton et al.
papers.summary: Does apathy, the reduction in goal-directed behavior, also dampen curiosity? Online observers (N=381) viewed familiar objects and realistic AI-generated novel ones, interacted with them, rated them, and completed apathy and curiosity questionnaires. Higher apathy went with rating novel objects as more familiar, spending less time viewing them, and reporting lower perceptual curiosity, with emotional apathy showing the most consistent relationship. The authors suggest a mechanism linking apathy to reduced engagement with perceptual novelty.
papers.abstract: The hallmark of apathy is diminished goal-directed behaviour, yet its relationship to curiosity - the intrinsic drive to explore novel information - remains untested. Here, we examined whether trait apathy is associated with diminished perceptual curiosity. We presented online observers (N = 381) with images of either familiar, everyday objects; or novel, AI-generated objects, which appeared entirely realistic, but do not in fact exist. Observers used their mouse to interact with each stimulus before rating its familiarity, interest, and appeal, and then completed validated measures of trait apathy and perceptual curiosity. Our data yielded three convergent findings. First, trait apathy was associated with differences in how novel and familiar objects were subjectively rated - specifically, as trait apathy increased, observers rated novel objects as more familiar, and familiar objects as more interesting. Second, trait apathy was associated with changes in objective behaviour, such that, as trait apathy increased, observers spent less time viewing novel objects. Finally, scores on trait measures of apathy and curiosity were negatively correlated, such that those who reported higher levels of trait apathy had lower levels of perceptual curiosity. Emotional apathy in particular had the most consistent relationship across both task-based and trait measures of perceptual curiosity. Together, these findings demonstrate that lower perceptual curiosity is a key feature of the apathetic trait, and propose the existence of a previously unrecognised mechanism that links apathy to reduced engagement with perceptual novelty. These results have broad implications for current frameworks of motivation and curiosity in both healthy individuals and clinical populations.

papers.title: Further predictors of iconicity
papers.authors: David M. Sidhu
papers.summary: Iconicity is how much a word's form resembles its meaning, like 'meow', and it's usually measured with participant ratings. Here the author tested a set of new predictors in English and found that iconic words are low in frequency but generally well known, tend to have more specific meanings (moderated by concreteness and part of speech), and are more polysemous and emotional. Apart from one exception, they weren't more systematic, which reinforces the view that iconicity is tied to how words are used and to words as depictions.
papers.abstract: Iconicity refers to a perceived resemblance between the form of a signal and its meaning (e.g., "meow" resembling the sound of a cat). Iconicity has been operationalized by having participants rate words in terms of their iconicity. This has enabled researchers to examine the lexical and semantic properties of words high and low in iconicity, for example finding that iconic words tend to be rich in sensory experience and semantically unique. In the present study I examined a suite of novel predictors that have not been examined in English iconicity. I discovered that while iconic words are low in frequency they are generally well known. They also tend to have more specific meanings, though this was moderated by concreteness and part of speech. Iconic words are also more polysemous and emotional. With one exception, there was no evidence that iconic words were more systematic. Together these results extend previous work, and reinforce the finding that iconicity must be understood through a lens of word use and of words as depictions.

papers.title: Dissociating accuracy and metacognition in nutritional judgements
papers.authors: Kelly Hoogervorst, Francesco Bavato, Ashley Tyrer et al.
papers.summary: Thirty-two volunteers did a new two-choice task called MetaBites, comparing foods on either calorie density or nutritional quality (via the NRF 9.3 index) and rating their confidence at the trial, block and task level. People were more accurate when judging nutritional quality but felt more confident about calorie judgements, even though their metacognitive efficiency was the same across conditions. Familiarity pushed choices in opposite directions (familiar foods seen as more nutritious and less calorie-dense), while liking drove confidence, so different cues seem to shape what people choose and how sure they feel.
papers.abstract: The gap between nutritional knowledge and dietary behaviour remains poorly understood, yet may partly reflect systematic biases in how individuals evaluate food and assess their own nutritional judgements. Here, we introduce the MetaBites task, a novel two-alternative forced-choice paradigm assessing nutritional judgements under adaptive difficulty control. Thirty-two healthy volunteers compared foods on either caloric density or nutritional quality, the latter quantified using the Nutrient-Rich Foods (NRF) 9.3 index. Participants provided trial-level, block-level, and task-level confidence ratings, enabling assessment of metacognitive monitoring across multiple levels. The task showed adequate validity, supported by staircase convergence, a clear speed-accuracy trade-off, and higher confidence on correct relative to incorrect trials. Results revealed a dissociation across conditions: participants showed higher objective performance when judging nutritional quality, yet reported significantly higher confidence for calorie judgements, and task-level global confidence decreased significantly in the NRF condition but remained stable for calorie judgements. Metacognitive efficiency did not differ between conditions. Familiarity with food items was associated with choice behaviour in opposing directions across conditions, consistent with a tendency to perceive familiar foods as more nutritious and less calorie-dense. Liking rather than familiarity was associated with higher trial-level confidence. Together, these findings show that objective performance and subjective confidence can dissociate in nutritional judgements, with distinct heuristic cues shaping choice and confidence. The MetaBites task offers a promising tool for investigating metacognitive contributions to nutritional decision-making in both healthy and clinical populations.

papers.title: Beyond attention: performance pressure shifts information-processing complexity
papers.authors: Laura Voigt, Arne Nieuwenhuys, Rich S.W. Masters et al.
papers.summary: Why does pressure make some people choke and others excel? This proposal argues that pressure changes how complex the rules are that people use to guide action. Performance gets better when the shift matches the task's needs, and worse when it leads to oversimplifying, overcomplicating, or relying on rules that demand more processing resources than are available. It frames pressure as something beyond an attention effect.
papers.abstract: Why does performance pressure sometimes cause choking but sometimes elicit exceptional performance? We propose that pressure shifts the complexity of information-processing rules that guide action. Performance improves when shifts move processing toward task-matched complexity and deteriorates when they promote maladaptive simplification, overcomplexification, or the use of rules that exceed available processing resources.

papers.title: Adapting to linguistic innovations: the role of language contact in bilingual and monolingual speakers
papers.authors: Helen Engemann, Ioli Baroncini
papers.summary: Two experiments looked at how speakers pick up innovative ways of describing motion events in Italian. Both German-Italian bilinguals and Italian monolinguals adapted to the innovative structures at an abstract level, but only bilinguals with a lot of German contact kept the change at a later post-test. That points to bilingual experience as a factor in how language innovations spread, which is a nice link between interaction-level adaptation and long-term language change.
papers.abstract: Contact between speakers and languages may play a key role in driving language change. During interaction, speakers tend to adapt to their interlocutors' speech, which can cumulatively lead to longer-term changes. Yet it remains unclear how innovations emerge, and who drives their adoption. These questions are addressed through two experiments on Italian motion-events framing. Study 1 examines German-Italian bilinguals with varying cumulative German contact, exploring whether exposure to innovative satellite-framed constructions triggers adaptation within Italian and across languages. Study 2 tests Italian monolinguals to assess adaptation in the absence of cross-linguistic influence. Results show that both bilinguals and monolinguals adapt to innovative structures at an abstract level, but only bilinguals with a high degree of German contact maintain these changes in a post-test, highlighting the role of bilingual experience. Findings suggest language contact may enhance the uptake of innovations, providing insight into the cognitive mechanisms underlying language change.

papers.title: Set-size effects for complex objects in Developmental Prosopagnosia: visual search for faces, words and cars
papers.authors: Hyeongmin Kim, Andrea Albonico, Jennifer Hemström et al.
papers.abstract: Whether developmental prosopagnosia is specific to faces is an ongoing controversy. One difficulty that may contribute to discrepant results is differences in tests used to assess face and object processing. Here, we devised a search test to measure the efficiency of processing for faces, cars, and words. We had 14 subjects with developmental prosopagnosia and 26 controls perform three search tests. For face-search, subjects saw an array ranging from three to seven faces and had to answer whether all depicted the same person or if one was a different person. Similar tests were constructed for cars and words. The main variables were response time and the set-size effect, which refers to the additional time required for every additional stimulus in the array. At the group level, the prosopagnosic subjects were impaired in face search but no different from controls on car or word search. However, at a single-subject level, only 20% had evidence of a putative classical dissociation to support claims that their recognition disorder is face-specific, while 30% had abnormally prolonged car-search times, and 50% had indeterminate results. The results align with a meta-analysis that concluded there was heterogeneity in object recognition in developmental prosopagnosia.
papers.summary: To get at whether developmental prosopagnosia (lifelong difficulty recognizing faces) is specific to faces, the researchers built matched visual search tests for faces, cars, and words. Fourteen people with prosopagnosia and 26 controls judged whether all items in arrays of three to seven were the same or one differed, and the key measure was how much extra time each added item cost. As a group, the prosopagnosic participants were impaired only on faces, but individually just 20% showed a clear face-specific pattern, 30% were abnormally slow on cars, and 50% were indeterminate. That fits an earlier meta-analysis suggesting object recognition varies quite a bit within this population.

papers.title: Rightward saccades distort the scaffold of spatial working memory in ADHD
papers.authors: Simar Moussaoui, Adam Frost, Matthias Niemeier
papers.summary: People with ADHD did a spatial memory task in which they remembered one or three item locations across leftward, rightward, or no eye movements, and their results were compared with a neurotypical sample. After rightward saccades they showed bigger systematic distortions in remembered locations than after leftward ones, and they lacked the usual load-related increase in unsystematic error. The authors offer two explanations, weaker right-hemisphere contributions or a destabilised spatial anchor, and describe the pattern as a partial neglect-like vulnerability that isn't just a capacity limit.
papers.abstract: Attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) is typically characterized by executive dysfunction, yet emerging evidence points to spatially asymmetrical features of cognition. We examined whether transsaccadic working memory (tWM), the mechanism that integrates visual and motor signals across eye movements, shows directional vulnerability in ADHD. Participants with ADHD completed a spatial tWM task in which memory arrays (one or three items) were presented before leftward, rightward, or fixation trials, and repositioned a probe to the remembered target location. For comparison, data from a previously tested neurotypical sample were included in group-level analyses. Errors were decomposed into systematic and unsystematic components. Compared to controls, ADHD participants showed a modest but reliable rightward-saccade disadvantage, with greater systematic distortions after rightward than leftward eye movements. Saccades disrupted working memory in both groups, but the typical load-dependent increase in unsystematic error observed in neurotypical participants was absent in ADHD. Two complementary interpretations may account for this asymmetry. The integration-imbalance hypothesis attributes it to weakened right-hemisphere contributions to spatial working memory, which impair integration of left-hemisphere oculomotor and right-hemisphere spatial signals during rightward saccades. Alternatively, the anchoring-disruption hypothesis suggests that rightward eye movements destabilize the spatial scaffold anchoring remembered locations, producing geometric distortions without increased error. Together, these findings identify a direction-specific fragility of visuomotor-cognitive coupling in ADHD not explained by general capacity limits. More broadly, they reveal a partial neglect-like pattern of transsaccadic vulnerability: selective impairment for rightward saccades without a left-field deficit, highlighting the utility of oculomotor paradigms for revealing hidden spatial asymmetries in neurocognitive function.

papers.title: Semantic working memory supports phrasal planning: Evidence from acute stroke
papers.authors: Rachel Zahn, Heather Dial, Tatiana Schnur et al.
papers.summary: In people tested soon after a left-hemisphere stroke, semantic working memory capacity predicted how accurately they produced phrases, especially noun phrases with two adjectives, even after accounting for single-word abilities. Phonological working memory didn't predict production accuracy. This fits the idea that we plan the meaning of speech phrase by phrase, holding several word meanings active in a semantic buffer before speaking.
papers.abstract: This study examined the contribution of semantic and phonological working memory (WM) to lexical-semantic planning during language production for individuals tested acutely after left-hemisphere stroke. Participants completed tasks assessing phrase and sentence production, single-word retrieval, semantic and phonological WM, and single-word input processing. Using a constrained production paradigm that manipulated structure (phrase vs. sentence) and number of adjectival modifiers (one vs. two), we found that semantic WM capacity, indexed by performance on a category probe task, predicted accuracy in producing phrases containing multiple content words, even after controlling for single-word processing abilities. In contrast, phonological WM capacity, indexed by performance on a digit matching span task, did not relate to production accuracy. The relation to semantic WM was specific to the condition with the largest number of content words within a phrase (two-adjective noun phrase). These findings support the contention that lexical-semantic planning occurs phrase by phrase and is constrained by the capacity of a semantic maintenance buffer that supports activation and maintenance of multiple lexical-semantic representations prior to articulation. In contrast, phonological planning appears to operate within a narrower window that makes few demands on phonological WM. The results converge with prior neuropsychological evidence linking semantic WM to phrase-level planning and further imply that the phrase serves as the default scope of lexical-semantic encoding in production. Implications for models of WM and language production are discussed.

papers.title: Ventral striatal and caudate contributions to episodic retrieval
papers.authors: Tobias Sommer, Anne Bierbrauer, Matthias Gamer et al.
papers.summary: An fMRI study used a word-picture learning task with two cued-recall tests 24 hours apart, and participants rated how specific their memories were. Caudate activity during successful recall looked more like pre-retrieval control or orienting to salient memories than effortful post-retrieval control. Ventral striatal activity tracked the gap between expected and actual reward from retrieval, a kind of metacognitive reward prediction error, and also signalled relevance and affected re-encoding to help future retrieval.
papers.abstract: Striatal activity during episodic memory retrieval is a robust phenomenon observed across various stimulus types and experimental paradigms. Previous research suggests that the ventral striatum and the caudate contribute differentially to retrieval processes: ventral striatal activity is posited to vary with the intrinsic reward of successful retrieval, whereas caudate activity is attributed to effortful cognitive control. The present fMRI study aimed to test the overarching hypothesis that these striatal subregions make distinct contributions to episodic retrieval and to further specify their functional roles. To this end, we employed a word-picture paired-associates learning paradigm in which words served as cues in two consecutive cued-recall tests that were separated by 24 h. Participants indicated the specificity of their associative memories, enabling characterization of striatal response profiles as a function of associative memory specificity and treatment of memory specificity as a proxy for the intrinsic reward associated with retrieval success. Rather than being not readily compatible with a role of the caudate in effortful post-retrieval control, the results suggest that elevated caudate activity during successful recall reflects pre-retrieval control or involuntary orienting to salient mnemonic information. In contrast, rather than reflect intrinsic reward itself, ventral striatal activity varied with the discrepancy between expected and actual intrinsic reward elicited by retrieval outcomes-that is, a metacognitive reward prediction error. Moreover, ventral striatum signaled the relevance of retrieved information and modulated its re-encoding to facilitate future retrievals.

papers.title: Individual differences in motor and auditory activation in second language speech learning: Roles of domain-general auditory processing.
papers.authors: Kazuya Saito-van Poeteren, Adam Tierney, Kotaro Takizawa et al.
papers.summary: Looking at 207 Japanese learners of English, researchers combined behavior and fMRI to see how auditory precision relates to brain activity and learning of the English vowels [æ] and [ʌ]. Learners with lower auditory precision had weaker vowel proficiency and more sensorimotor activation when discriminating those vowels, but not for comparable nonspeech sounds. Learners with higher precision did better and showed less motor activity, which may mean the less precise learners lean on first-language articulatory routines.
papers.abstract: While existing models emphasize the critical roles of auditory and motor systems in speech perception, it remains unclear how individual learners differentially rely on these systems and how their relative weighting relates to language learning. This study investigates the neural mechanisms through which individual differences in domain-general auditory processing influence reliance on these networks during second language (L2) phonetic learning. Focusing on the acquisition of English [æ] and [ʌ] by 207 Japanese learners, we examined participants with varying auditory precision profiles using both behavioral and functional magnetic resonance imaging analyses as they performed discrimination tasks for speech and nonverbal sounds. The findings revealed a pattern consistent with a triangular relationship among learners' auditory precision, brain activation in motor-related regions, and L2 speech development. Learners with lower auditory precision tended to show less advanced L2 vowel proficiency and exhibited higher levels of sensorimotor activation during discrimination of English [æ] and [ʌ], but not during discrimination of nonspeech counterparts with comparable second formant variation. In light of theoretical accounts of adult L2 speech learning (Best & Tyler, 2007), one possible interpretation is that greater reliance on articulatory processing among less auditory-precise and less experienced or proficient L2 learners reflects the processing of L2 sounds through first language articulatory routines. In contrast, learners with higher auditory precision attained not only more advanced L2 vowel proficiency but also lower levels of sensorimotor activity, comparable to that observed during nonverbal processing, suggesting more balanced spectrotemporal and articulatory analyses of sounds, which optimize both the process and outcomes of L2 speech learning. papers.title: Color desaturation in the periphery is explained by general mechanisms of contrast sensitivity and constancy.
papers.authors: Ana Rozman, Jasna Martinovic
papers.summary: Colors look washed out in peripheral vision, and this work asks whether that's special to color. Twenty participants matched perceived contrast of smaller, off-center discs to a standard disc, and both chromatic and luminance discs lost perceived contrast when small, with the loss shrinking as contrast went up, as contrast constancy predicts. Blurred edges also reduced perceived contrast a lot, so the authors conclude color and luminance in the periphery follow the same general rules of contrast sensitivity and constancy.
papers.abstract: = 20) matched the perceived contrast of a parafoveally presented comparison disc (2°-0.33°) to a standard 2° disc. For chromatic stimuli, perceived contrast decreased with decreasing size. A similar decrease in perceived contrast occurred for salience-equated luminance-defined discs. Loss of perceived contrast reduced as standard stimulus contrast increased, in line with contrast constancy theory, which predicts constant appearance for stimuli that are sufficiently distant from threshold. Since chromatic contrast sensitivity is reduced away from the fovea and color gamut has a lower range compared with luminance gamut, contrast constancy for color is unachievable within the monitor gamut for small isoluminant patches. Blurred edge discs had substantially reduced perceived contrast, reflecting the important role played by higher spatial frequency channels in defining contrast salience for luminance and color alike. In conclusion, the appearance of color and luminance in the periphery is affected similarly, implying that the process is governed by general laws of contrast sensitivity and constancy. papers.title: Ensemble averaging of symbolic numbers: Criterion mean judgments beat heuristics
papers.authors: Daniel Fitousi, Hadar Srulovich
papers.summary: Can people really compute the average of a set of digits, or do they use shortcuts? Participants saw four digits and judged whether their mean was above or below 5. Accuracy and speed tracked distance of the mean from 5 better than heuristics like the most extreme digit or the majority above or below, and this held even in a second experiment where those shortcuts were uninformative or misleading. The results support real mean-based integration of symbolic numbers, with heuristics playing only a secondary role under higher uncertainty.
papers.abstract: Can observers compute an ensemble mean from symbolic numbers, or is averaging-like performance driven by heuristic shortcuts? We addressed this question using a criterion-based design that yields clear predictions for mean-based integration. In two experiments, participants viewed a 2 × 2 array of four Arabic digits and decided, while timed, whether the arithmetic mean of the set was smaller or larger than 5. In Experiment 1 ( N = 40 ), accuracy and response time showed a robust ensemble-distance effect: decisions were slowest and least accurate when the set mean was closest to 5 and improved monotonically with mean distance. Item-level model comparisons further indicated that mean distance explained behavior better than prominent heuristic alternatives based on the most extreme digit or the majority of digits above versus below the criterion, and within-set dispersion produced an additional, independent impairment. Experiment 2 ( N = 40 ) provided a stronger diagnostic test by constructing stimulus regimes that rendered heuristic cues uninformative (majority ties) or misleading (extreme-item conflict) while matching mean distance and dispersion across regimes. Across regimes, model comparisons again favored mean distance for both accuracy and response time. Critically, the distance effect persisted when majority information carried no diagnostic value and when the most extreme digit favored the incorrect response. These results support genuine mean-based integration of symbolic magnitudes, while showing that heuristic strategies have only a secondary role apparent only under increased uncertainty. papers.title: Simulated responses from large language models are weak proxies for human economic preferences across 74 countries
papers.authors: Fadong Chen, Qijun Wang, Lei Wang et al.
papers.summary: Researchers ran a virtual Global Preference Survey, having LLMs simulate six economic preferences for 67,201 matched human respondents across 74 countries. The models captured modest individual-level alignment and recovered the direction of demographic effects such as gender, age and cognitive ability about 78% of the time, but only about 48% for cultural dimensions, with weaker alignment in less developed, less digitally connected countries. So LLM-simulated responses aren't yet reliable stand-ins for representative cross-national surveys.
papers.abstract: Large-scale surveys are central to investigating economic preferences but are costly and slow. Can large language model (LLM)-simulated responses substitute for human survey data? We conducted a virtual Global Preference Survey, simulating six experimentally validated economic preferences for 67,201 matched human respondents across 74 countries. Across 20 LLM configurations with diverse prompts and robustness checks, we found systematic but modest individual-level alignment (87.5% of Spearman correlations have 95% confidence intervals (CIs) above zero), with LLMs recovering the direction of associations in 77.8% (95% CI, (71.6%, 83.1%); CI-based consistency ratio) of gender, age and cognitive-ability dimensions, but only 48.1% (95% CI, (45.1%, 51.2%)) of cultural dimensions. Ablation and error decompositions suggest weaker alignment when removing demographic information than when removing country labels, and in many models alignment is weaker in economically undeveloped and less digitally connected countries. LLM-simulated responses may recover some individual- and group-level patterns but are not yet reliable proxies for cross-national representative surveys in macro-level inference or policy evaluation. Simulating a global survey of economic preferences across 74 countries, this study shows that large language models reproduce some demographic patterns in human preferences but fail to capture cultural differences, especially in lower-income countries.

papers.title: Circadian timing does not modulate human temporal contrast sensitivity
papers.authors: Hannah Sophie Heinrichs, Manuel Spitschan
papers.summary: To separate circadian from sleep-wake effects on vision, twelve participants followed a 40-hour forced desynchrony protocol while repeatedly doing temporal contrast sensitivity tasks for luminance and chromatic modulations at 2 and 8 Hz. Despite strong melatonin rhythms, Bayesian model comparison gave decisive evidence against circadian modulation of cone-mediated sensitivity. Earlier time-of-day effects may instead come from homeostatic factors, pupil-linked changes in retinal illuminance, or other pathways.
papers.abstract: Previous studies have reported diurnal variations in color perception and luminance contrast sensitivity, suggesting modulation of visual processing by the circadian pacemaker. To clarify potential time-of-day effects, we examined whether cone-mediated temporal contrast sensitivity is modulated by circadian timing. We disentangled circadian and homeostatic influences on human visual performance using a 40-hour forced desynchrony protocol. Twelve participants (five female participants, 24.4 ± 2.9 years, range 19-30) followed a repeating 3.75-hour cycle comprising 2 hours 30 minutes of wakefulness and 1 hour 15 minutes of sleep under constant environmental conditions. Circadian period was estimated from up to 46 salivary melatonin samples per participant. During wake periods, participants repeatedly completed temporal contrast sensitivity tasks at 2 Hz and 8 Hz, using tasks that probed both luminance (L+M+S) and chromatic (L-M, S-cone-directed) modulations. We tested for circadian modulation of visual performance by comparing hierarchical cosinor models with intercept-only null models using Bayes factors. All participants showed robust melatonin rhythms (mean τ = 24.18 ± 0.39 hours). Bayesian inference provided decisive evidence against circadian variation in luminance or chromatic contrast sensitivity. Within this controlled protocol, we found no detectable near-24-hour modulation of cone-mediated temporal contrast sensitivity. Previously reported time-of-day effects may instead reflect homeostatic influences, pupil-linked changes in retinal illuminance, or mechanisms outside the cone-mediated pathways probed here. By separating circadian phase from sleep-wake-related influences, this study clarifies when circadian modulation of visual performance can and cannot be inferred.

papers.title: Linking visual span and reading speed in dyslexia
papers.authors: Nilsu Atilgan, Ben D. Sawyer, Gordon E. Legge
papers.summary: Adults with dyslexia read more slowly and had narrower visual spans (the number of letters identified reliably in a single fixation) than typical readers, and span size correlated with reading speed. The team then adapted the measure for online testing, validated it in typical readers, and found the same pattern in a larger online sample with self-reported dyslexia. The authors present this as the first direct evidence that reduced visual span is a reliable feature of dyslexia, and as a scalable online way to study it.
papers.abstract: This study examines visual processing in dyslexia using a psychophysical measure linked to reading speed, the visual span, defined as the number of letters reliably identified within a single fixation. We asked whether reduced visual span is associated with slower reading in dyslexia. In a laboratory study, adults with dyslexia and typical readers completed standardized assessments, reading speed, and visual span measurements. Individuals with dyslexia showed significantly slower reading speeds and narrower visual span profiles than typical readers. Visual span size was positively correlated with reading speed across participants. The paradigm was then adapted for online testing. In a validation study with typical readers, online visual span and reading speed test showed patterns consistent with laboratory patterns, including a strong positive relationship between visual span size and reading speed. Applying this paradigm to a larger online sample of individuals with self-reported dyslexia revealed markedly slower reading speeds, reduced visual span sizes, and a robust correlation between visual span and reading speed despite substantial individual variability. Together, these findings provide the first direct evidence that reduced visual span is a reliable characteristic of dyslexia and is closely linked to reading performance. Moreover, they demonstrate that a brief, psychophysically grounded visual span assessment can be implemented reliably online, enabling scalable investigation of visual factors in dyslexia across diverse populations.

papers.title: Anisotropic speed discrimination sensitivity for expanding and contracting optic flow
papers.authors: Junxiang Luo, Hiroshi Ashida, Isao Yokoi et al.
papers.summary: Although forward movement produces expanding optic flow, some studies find people are more sensitive to contracting flow, so this work compared speed discrimination for the two. Sensitivity was similar at low and high speeds but better for contraction at an intermediate speed matching walking, in both planar 2D and simulated 3D flow. The authors suggest this could be an adaptive mechanism supporting balance during rare backward self-motion.
papers.abstract: Retinal optic flow provides critical visual cues for locomotion and self-navigation. Forward self-motion, such as walking or driving, typically induces an expanding radial flow pattern on the retina. Despite the predominance of expanding optic flow in everyday self-motion, several studies have reported higher sensitivity for contracting flow that arises under relatively rare conditions, such as walking backward or falling onto one's back. The underlying basis of this anisotropy remains elusive. In this study, we compared discrimination sensitivity to speed for expanding versus contracting optic flow, given that speed is a fundamental attribute of motion and that sensitivity to it provides insight into underlying visual mechanisms. We found that sensitivity in speed discrimination was comparable between expansion and contraction at low and high speeds but was significantly higher for contraction at an intermediate speed corresponding to ecologically relevant self-motion, such as walking. This anisotropic pattern was observed for both two-dimensional planar (Experiment 1) and simulated three-dimensional (Experiment 2) optic flow stimuli. Together, these findings suggest that anisotropic speed discrimination sensitivity to expanding and contracting optic flow at ecologically typical egomotion speeds may reflect an adaptive visual mechanism that supports postural stability and balance during relatively rare backward self-motion.

papers.title: Binocular summation of suprathreshold color
papers.authors: Frederick A. A. Kingdom, Donald Chang, Obai Osman
papers.summary: Binocular summation, the advantage of two eyes over one, has been measured for color only at threshold, so this work measured it at threshold and above using black-white, red-cyan and violet-lime Gabor patches on various pedestal contrasts. Summation held across the whole range of pedestals and was stronger for the two chromatic directions than for black-white. Of four models tested, a three-parameter additive model and a four-parameter model with binocular adding and differencing channels (Max(S+S-)) fit best and equally well.
papers.abstract: Two eyes are better than one for detecting both achromatic and chromatic contrast, an advantage termed binocular summation. It is widely believed that binocular summation is mediated by neurons that sum the signals from the two eyes. While binocular summation for luminance-defined stimuli has been measured for both threshold and increment-threshold contrasts, those for chromatic stimuli have only been measured at threshold contrasts. Here we measured binocular summation for both threshold and increment-threshold contrasts defined along the black-white, red-cyan, and violet-lime axes of cone-contrast color space. Stimuli were 1.0 cycles per degree Gabor patches at a range of pedestal contrasts, each presented to both eyes, added to which was an increment to the left, right or both eyes. Left eye and right eye data were combined, and binocular summation was calculated as the ratio of monocular to binocular increment thresholds. For all three color directions, binocular summation was observed throughout the range of pedestal contrasts, with greater summation for the red-cyan and violet-lime compared with the black-white color directions. Four models of binocular summation were tested: a probability and an additive summation model each with two free parameters, a three-free-parameter model of additive summation, and a four-free-parameter model based on the modelled responses of binocular adding and binocular differencing channels, termed Max(S + S -). The three-free-parameter additive and Max(S+S-) models fared best and equally well.
